This is the longest method we have seen so far, so we shall break it down into more manageable pieces:

*   The header indicates that the method has a `void` return type, and that it takes no parameters.
*   The body comprises eight statements plus associated comments.
*   The first six statements are responsible for printing what you see in the BlueJ terminal window: five lines of text and a sixth blank line.
*   The seventh statement adds the balance inserted by the customer (through previous calls to `insertMoney`) to the running total of all money collected so far by the machine.
*   The eighth statement resets the balance to zero with a basic assignment statement, in preparation for the next customer.

By comparing the output that appears with the statements that produced it, it is easy to see that a statement such as

```
System.out.println("# The BlueJ Line");
```

literally prints the string that appears between the matching pair of double-quote characters. The basic form of a call to `println` is

```
System.out.println(something-we-want-to-print);
```

where *something-we-want-to-print* can be replaced by any string, enclosed between a pair of double-quote characters. There is nothing significant in the “#” character that is in the string—it is simply one of the characters we wish to be printed. All the printing statements in the `printTicket` method are calls to the `println` method of the `System.out` object that is built into the Java language, and what appears between the round brackets is the parameter to each method call, as you might expect.

In the fourth statement, the argument to `println` is a little more complicated and requires some more explanation:

```
System.out.println("# " + price + " cents.");
```

What it does is print out the price of the ticket, with some extra characters on either side of the price amount. The two “+” operators are being used to construct a single argument value, in the form of a string, from three separate components:

*   the string literal: `"# "` (*note the space character after the hash*);
*   the value of the `price` field (note that there are no quotes around the field name because we want the field’s value, not its name);
*   the string literal: `" cents."` (note the space character before the word `"cents"`).

When used between a string and anything else, + is a string-concatenation operator rather than an arithmetic-addition operator; that is, it concatenates (joins) strings together to create a new string. The numeric value of `price` is automatically converted into a string and joined to the two surrounding strings.

Note that the final call to `println` contains no argument value. This is allowed, and the result of calling it will be to leave a blank line between the previous output and any that follows. You will easily see the blank line if you print a second ticket.

# 2.10: Method summary

It is worth summarizing a few features of methods at this point, because methods are fundamental to the programs we will be writing and exploring in this book. They implement the core actions of every object.

A method with parameters receives argument values passed to it from the method’s caller, and the method will then use those values to help it perform a specific task. Not all methods take parameters; many simply use the data stored in the object’s fields to carry out their task.

If a method has a non-`void` return type, it will return some data to the place it was called from—and that data will almost certainly be used in the caller for further calculations or program manipulations. Many methods, though, have a `void` return type and return nothing, but they still perform a useful task within the context of their object. Methods that change the state of an object—mutator methods—usually have a `void` return type. They often take parameters whose values are used in the modification, although it is still possible to write a mutating method that does not take parameters.

An accessor method (such as a getter method) always has a non-`void` return type and returns a value related to an object’s state.

# 2.11: Summary of the naïve ticket machine

We have now examined the internal structure of the naïve `TicketMachine` class in some detail. We have seen that the class has a small outer layer that simply gives a name to the class, and a more substantial inner body containing fields, a constructor, and several methods. Fields are used to store data that enable objects to maintain a state that persists between method calls. Each object has its own copy of the fields and so these variables are also called instance variables.

Constructors are used to set up an initial state when an object is created. Having a proper initial state will enable an object to respond appropriately to method calls immediately following its creation.

Methods implement the defined behavior of the class’s objects. Accessor methods provide information about an object’s state, and mutator methods change an object’s state.

We have seen that constructors are distinguished from methods by having the same name as the class in which they are defined. Both constructors and methods may take parameters, but only methods may have a return type. Non-`void` return types allow us to pass a value out of a method to the place from where the method was called. It is important to appreciate that 'returning a value' does not mean that the value is printed. Although BlueJ brings up a Method Result dialog window when a non-`void` method is called interactively, that is purely as a visual aid and not part of the normal program behavior.

A method with a non-`void` return type must have at least one return statement in its body; this will usually be the final statement. Constructors never have a return type of any sort—not even `void`.

Before attempting the following exercises, be sure that you have a good understanding of how ticket machines behave and how that behavior is implemented through the fields, constructor, and methods of the class.

# 2.12: Reflecting on the design of the ticket machine

From studying the internals of the `TicketMachine` class, you should have come to appreciate how inadequate it would be in the real world. It is deficient in several ways:

*   It contains no check that the customer has entered enough money to pay for a ticket.
*   It does not refund any money if the customer pays too much for a ticket.
*   It does not check to ensure that the customer inserts sensible amounts of money. (If you haven't already done so, experiment with what happens if a negative amount is entered, for instance.)
*   It does not check that the ticket price passed to its constructor is sensible.

If we could remedy these problems, then we would have a much more functional piece of software that could serve as the basis for operating a real-world ticket machine.

In the next few sections, we shall examine the implementation of an improved ticket machine class that attempts to deal with some of the inadequacies of the naïve implementation.

Open the *better-ticket-machine* project. As before, this project contains a single class: `TicketMachine`. Before looking at the internal details of the class, experiment with it by creating some instances and see whether you notice any differences in behavior between this version and the previous naïve version.

One difference is that the new version has an additional method, `refund-Balance`. Take a look at what happens when you call it after inserting some money.

The first significant change can be seen in the `insertMoney` method. We recognized that the main problem with the naïve ticket machine was its failure to check certain conditions. One of those missing checks was on the amount of money inserted by a customer, as it was possible for a negative amount of money to be inserted. We have remedied that failing by making use of a *conditional statement* to check that the amount inserted has a value greater than zero:

```
if(amount > 0) {
    balance = balance + amount;
}
else {
    System.out.println("Use a positive amount rather than: " +
                       amount);
}
```

Conditional statements are also known as *if-statements*, from the keyword used to introduce them. The test used in a conditional statement is an example of a *boolean expression.* Earlier in this chapter, we introduced arithmetic expressions that produced numerical results. A boolean expression has only two possible values (`true` or `false`): the value of `amount` is either greater than zero (`true`) or it is not greater (`false`). A conditional statement makes use of those two possible values to choose between two different actions. This kind of either/or decision should be familiar from situations in everyday life: for instance, if I have an assignment to complete, then I shall work on my assignment; otherwise, I shall visit a friend.

A conditional statement has the general form described in the following *pseudo-code*:

```
if(perform some test that gives a true or false result) {
    Do the statements here if the test gave a true result
}
else {
    Do the statements here if the test gave a false result
}
```

Certain parts of this pseudocode are proper Java code, and those will appear in almost all conditional statements—the keywords `if` and `else`, the round brackets around the test, and the curly brackets marking the two blocks—while the other three italicized parts will be fleshed out differently for each situation being coded. Only one of the two blocks of statements following the test will ever be performed following the evaluation of the test.

In the `insertMoney` method, following the test of an inserted amount, we shall only either add the amount to the balance or print the error message. The test uses the *greater-than operator*, “>”, to compare the value in `amount` against `0`. If the value is greater than zero, then it is added to the balance. If it is not greater than zero, then an error message is printed. By using a conditional statement, we have, in effect, protected the `balance` field from being changed in the case where the parameter does not represent a valid amount.

Three other "relational operators" are “<” (less-than), “<=” (less-than or equal-to), and “>=” (greater-than or equal-to). These all give a result of either true or false and all are used to compare numeric values, as in the `printTicket` method.

There are two further relational operators: “`==`” (equal-to) and “`!=`” (not-equal-to). Note that two “=” characters next to each other, rather than a single “=” character, are used to test for equality because the single one is used for assignment. It is common for these different operators to be mixed up because we are used to thinking of “=” as meaning “equal-to”, which it does not in Java.

Details of other Java operators can be found in [**Appendix C**](#urn_pearson_manifest_6d1eb3ef-4b9f-41bb-bba5-a8c39c999ddc.xhtml).

# 2.14: A further conditional-statement example

The `printTicket` method contains a further example of a conditional statement. Here it is in outline:

```
if(balance >= price) {

    Printing details omitted.

    // Update the total collected with the price.
    total = total + price;
    // Reduce the balance by the price.
    balance = balance – price;
}
else {
    System.out.printf("You must insert at least %d more cents.%n",
                      price – balance);
}
```

With this if-statement, we have fixed the problem that the naïve version makes no check that a customer has inserted enough money for a ticket before printing. This version checks that the value in the `balance` field is greater-than or equal-to the value in the `price` field. If it is, then it is okay to print a ticket. If it is not, then we print an error message instead.

The printing of the error message introduces the `printf` method as an alternative to `println` to print the message. This was introduced in [**Exercise 2.43**](#urn_pearson_manifest_e3be5454-ce35-4a7f-8d1b-b390f3cb3c2e.xhtml). The `printf` method provides a “formatted print” of a string. Its first parameter is an outline of the overall string to be printed in the form of a *format string*. The format string contains *format specifiers* `(%d` and `%n`) which are placeholders for values to be inserted in the output. In this case `%d` is a placeholder for a decimal integer and `%n` is a placeholder to end the line. Values to insert into the placeholders follow the format string in the call to `printf`, except that `%n` does not need a corresponding value. So:

```
System.out.printf("%n");
```

is equivalent to:

```
System.out.println();
```

In the use of `printf` in the `printTicket` method, the `%d` will be replaced by the value of the expression `price – balance`.

The `printTicket` method reduces the value of `balance` by the value of `price`. Consequently, if a customer inserts more money than the price of the ticket, then some money will be left in the balance that could be used toward the price of a second ticket. Alternatively, the customer could ask to be refunded the remaining balance, and that is what the `refundBalance` method does, as we shall see in [**section 2.16**](#urn_pearson_manifest_b31a44e0-c442-4b1b-b308-d66aa3482f39.xhtml).

# 2.15: Scope highlighting

You will have noticed by now that the BlueJ editor displays source code with some additional decoration: colored boxes around some elements, such as methods and if-statements (see, for example, **Code 2.8**).

These colored annotations are known as *scope highlighting*, and they help clarify logical units of your program. A *scope* (also called a *block*) is a unit of code usually indicated by a pair of curly brackets. The whole body of a class is a scope, as is the body of each method and the *if* and *else* parts of an if-statement.

As you can see, scopes are often nested: the if-statement is inside a method, which is inside a class. BlueJ helps by distinguishing different kinds of scopes with different colors.

One of the most common errors in the code of beginning programmers is getting the curly brackets wrong—either by having them in the wrong place, or by having a bracket missing altogether. Two things can greatly help in avoiding this kind of error:

*   Pay attention to proper indentation of your code. Every time a new scope starts (after an open curly bracket), indent the following code one level more. Closing the scope brings the indentation back. If your indentation is completely out, use BlueJ’s “Auto-layout” function (find it in the editor menu!) to fix it.
*   Pay attention to the scope highlighting. You will quickly get used to the way well-structured code looks. Try removing a curly bracket in the editor or adding one at an arbitrary location and observe how the coloring changes. Get used to recognizing when scopes look wrong.

# 2.16: Local variables

So far, we have encountered two different kinds of variable: fields (instance variables) and parameters. We are now going to introduce a third kind. All have in common that they store data, but each has a particular role to play.

[**Section 2.7**](#urn_pearson_manifest_792c1eb7-301a-41a7-95f6-30e45686143a.xhtml) noted that a method body (or, in general, a *block*) can contain both declarations and statements. So far, none of the methods we have looked at contained any declarations but the `refundBalance` method does.

```
public int refundBalance()
{
    int amountToRefund;
    amountToRefund = balance;
    balance = 0;
    return amountToRefund;
}
```

It contains three statements and a single declaration. The statements assign the value of the `balance` field to the `amountToRefund` variable, then set `balance` to zero and, finally, return the value in `amountToRefund` which is, of course, the old value of `balance` before it was set to zero.

The declaration of `amountToRefund` at the start of the method introduces a new kind of variable. What kind of variable is it? We know that it is not a field, because fields are defined outside methods. It is also not a parameter, as those are always defined in the method header.

The `amountToRefund` variable is what is known as a *local variable* because it is defined locally inside a method body. The “local” designation refers to the fact that a local variable is only available to the code inside its defining block – in this case, the method body. A local variable cannot be accessed from any other method in the same class. This contrasts with fields, which can be accessed by every method in their class.

Local variable declarations look like field declarations, but they never have `private` or `public` as part of them. Both parameters and local variables have a scope that is limited to the statements of the method to which they belong. Their lifetime is the time of the method’s execution: they are created when a method is called and destroyed when a method finishes. Each call of the method creates a new copy of them.

It is quite common to initialize local variables within their declaration. So, we could merge the declaration and first statement of `refundBalance` as:

```
int amountToRefund = balance;
```

but it is still important to keep in mind that there are two steps going on here: declaring the variable `amountToRefund` and giving it an initial value.

You might wonder why there is a need for local variables if we have fields. Local variables are primarily used as temporary storage, to help a single method complete its task; we think of them as data storage for a single method. In contrast, fields are used to store data that persists through the whole life of an object. We try to avoid declaring as fields variables that only have a local (method-level) usage; that is, whose values do not have to be retained beyond a single method call. So even if two or more methods in the same class use local variables for a similar purpose, it is not appropriate to define them as fields if their values do not need to persist beyond the end of the methods.

The following exercises will help to illustrate how a local variable helps `refundBalance` to fulfill its task, as we try to write the method without using one.

# 2.17: Fields, parameters, and local variables

With the introduction of `amountToRefund` in the `refundBalance` method, we have now seen three different kinds of variables: fields, parameters, and local variables. It is important to understand the similarities and differences between these three kinds. Here is a summary of their features:

*   All three kinds of variables can store a value that is appropriate to their defined types. For instance, a defined type of `int` allows a variable to store an integer value.
*   Fields are defined outside constructors and methods.
*   Fields are used to store values that persist throughout the life of an object. As such, they maintain the current state of an object. They have a lifetime that lasts as long as their object lasts.
*   Fields have class scope: they are accessible throughout the whole class, so they can be used within any of the constructors or methods of the class in which they are defined.
*   As long as they are defined as `private`, fields cannot be accessed from anywhere outside their defining class.
*   Parameters and local variables persist only for the period that a constructor or method executes. Their lifetime is only as long as a single call, so their values are lost between calls. As such, they act as temporary rather than permanent storage locations.
*   Parameters are defined in the header of a constructor or method. They receive their values from outside, being initialized by the argument values that form part of the constructor or method call.
*   Parameters have a scope that is limited to their defining constructor or method.
*   Local variables are defined inside the body of a constructor or method. They can be initialized and used only within the body of their defining constructor or method. Local variables must be initialized before they are used in an expression—they are not given a default value.
*   Local variables have a scope that is limited to the block in which they are defined. They are not accessible from anywhere outside that block.

New programmers often find it difficult to work out whether a variable should be defined as a field or as a local variable. There is a temptation to define all variables as fields because they can be accessed from anywhere in the class. In fact, the opposite approach is a much better rule to adopt: define variables local to a method unless they are clearly a genuine part of an object’s persistent state. Even if you anticipate using the same variable in two or more methods, define a separate version locally to each method until you are sure that persistence between method calls is justified.

# 2.18: Summary of the better-ticket machine

In developing a better version of the `TicketMachine` class, we have been able to address the major inadequacies of the naïve version. In doing so, we have introduced two new language constructs: the conditional statement and local variables.

*   A conditional statement gives us a means to perform a test and then, based on the result of that test, perform either one or the other of two distinct actions.
*   Local variables allow us to calculate and store temporary values within a constructor or method. They contribute to the behavior that their defining method implements, but their values are lost once that constructor or method finishes its execution.

You can find more details of conditional statements and the form their tests can take in [**Appendix D**](#urn_pearson_manifest_e8177417-dca5-4772-862a-582d090c9baf.xhtml).

sum = 99 + 3;
```

You will see the following error message:

```
Error: cannot find symbol – variable sum
```

This is because Java requires that every variable (`sum`, in this case) be given a type before it can be used. Recall that every time a field, parameter, or local variable has been introduced for the first time in the source, it has had a type name in front of it, such as `int` or `String`. int sum = 0;
sum = 99 + 3;
```

This time there is no complaint, because `sum` has been introduced with a type and can be used without repeating the type thereafter. If you then type

```
sum
```

on a line by itself (with no semicolon), you will see the value it currently stores.

Now try this in the Code Pad:

```
String swimmer = "cat" + "fish";
swimmer
```

Once again, we have given an appropriate type to the variable `swimmer`, allowing us to make an assignment to it and find out what it stores. This time we chose to set it to the value we wanted at the same time as declaring it.

What would you expect to see after the following?

```
String fish = swimmer;
fish
```

Try it out. What do you think has happened in the assignment?

# 2.21: Summary

In this chapter, we have covered the basics of how to create a class definition. Classes contain fields, constructors, and methods that define the state and behavior of objects. Within the body of a constructor or method, a sequence of statements implements that part of its behavior. Local variables can be used as temporary data storage to assist with that. We have covered assignment statements and conditional statements and will be adding further types of statements in later chapters.

Terms introduced in this chapter:

1.  **field, instance variable, constructor, method, method header, method body, parameter, argument, accessor, getter, mutator, setter, declaration, initialization, block, statement, assignment statement, conditional statement, return statement, return type, comment, expression, boolean expression, operator, variable, local variable, scope, lifetime**

The following exercises are designed to help you experiment with the concepts of Java that we have discussed in this chapter. You will create your own classes that contain elements such as fields, constructors, methods, assignment statements, and conditional statements.

# Chapter 3 Object Interaction

In the previous chapters, we examined what objects are and how they are implemented. We discussed fields, constructors, and methods when we looked at class definitions.

We shall now go one step further. To construct interesting applications, it is not enough to build individual working objects. Instead, objects must be combined so that they cooperate to perform a common task. In this chapter, we shall build a small application from three objects and arrange for methods to call other methods to achieve their goal.

# 3.1: The clock example

The project we shall use to discuss interaction of objects is a display for a digital clock. The display shows hours and minutes, separated by a colon (**Figure 3.1**). For this exercise, we shall build a clock with a European-style 24-hour display. Thus, the display shows the time from 00:00 (midnight) to 23:59 (one minute before midnight). It turns out that building a 12-hour clock is slightly more difficult than a 24-hour clock and we shall leave that until the end of the chapter.

#### Figure 3.1 **A display of a digital clock**

![A clock, represented by a rectangular box, reads 11:03.](images/b819bc99-957e-4b4e-8076-972e5f0777e9_ASSET_FG_03_001.png "View Image")

# 3.2: Abstraction and modularization

A first idea might be to implement the whole clock display in a single class. That is, after all, what we have seen so far: how to build classes to do a job.

However, here we shall approach this problem slightly differently. We will see whether we can identify subcomponents in the problem that we can turn into separate classes. The reason is *complexity*. As we progress in this book, the examples we use and the programs we build will get more and more complex. Trivial tasks such as the ticket machine can be solved as a single problem. You can look at the complete task and devise a solution using a single class. For more complex problems, that is too simplistic. As a problem grows larger, it becomes increasingly difficult to keep track of all details at the same time.

The solution we use to deal with the complexity problem is *abstraction*. We divide the problem into sub-problems, then again into sub-sub-problems, and so on, until the individual problems are small enough to be easy to deal with. Once we solve one of the sub-problems, we do not think about the details of that part anymore but treat the solution as a single building block for our next problem. This technique is sometimes referred to as *divide and conquer*.

Let us discuss this with an example. Imagine engineers in a car company designing a new car. They may think about the parts of the car, such as the shape of the outer body, the size and location of the engine, the number and size of the seats in the passenger area, the exact spacing of the wheels, and so on. Another engineer, on the other hand, whose job is part of the team to design the engine thinks of the many parts of an engine: the cylinders, the injection mechanism, the carburetor, the electronics, etc. They will think of the engine not as a single entity, but as a complex work of many parts. One of these parts may be a spark plug.

Then there is an engineer (maybe in a different company) who designs the spark plug. They will think of the spark plug as a complex artifact of many parts. They might have conducted complex studies to determine exactly what kind of metal to use for the contacts, or what kind of material and production process to use for the insulation.

The same is true for many other parts. A designer at the highest level will regard a wheel as a single part. Another engineer much further down the chain may spend their days thinking about the chemical composition necessary to produce the right materials to make the tires. For the tire engineer, the tire is a complex thing. The car company will just buy the tire from the tire company and then view it as a single entity. This is abstraction.

The engineer in the car company *abstracts from* the details of the tire manufacture to be able to concentrate on the details of the construction of, say, the wheel. The designer designing the body shape of the car abstracts from the technical details of the wheels and the engine to concentrate on the design of the body (they will just be interested in the size of the engine and the wheels).

The same is true for every other component. While someone might be concerned with designing the interior passenger space, someone else may work on developing the fabric that will eventually be used to cover the seats.

The point is, if viewed in enough detail, a car consists of so many parts that it is practically impossible for a single person to know every detail about every part at the same time. If that were necessary, no car could ever be built.

The reason why cars are successfully built is that the engineers use *modularization* and abstraction. They divide the car into independent modules (wheel, engine, gear box, seat, steering wheel, etc.) and get separate people to work on separate modules independently. When a module is built, they use abstraction. They view that module as a single component that is used to build more-complex components.

Modularization and abstraction thus complement each other. Modularization is the process of dividing large things (problems) into smaller parts, while abstraction is the process of ignoring details to focus on the bigger picture.

# 3.3: Abstraction in software

The same principles of modularization and abstraction discussed in the previous section are used in software development. To help us maintain an overview in complex programs, we try to identify subcomponents that we can program as independent entities. Then we try to use those subcomponents as if they were simple parts, without being concerned about their inner complexities.

In object-oriented programming, these components and subcomponents are objects. If we were trying to construct a car in software, using an object-oriented language, we would try to do what the car engineers do. Instead of implementing the car as a single, monolithic object, we would first construct separate objects for an engine, gearbox, wheel, seat, and so on, and then assemble the car object from those smaller objects.

Identifying what kinds of objects (and with these, classes) you should have in a software system for any given problem is not always easy, and we shall have a lot more to say about that later in this book. For now, we shall start with a relatively simple example. So, back to our digital clock.

# 3.4: Modularization in the clock example

Let us have a closer look at the clock-display example. Using the abstraction concepts we have just described, we want to try to find the best way to view this example so that we can write some classes to implement it. One way to look at it is to consider it as consisting of a single display with four digits (two digits for the hours, two for the minutes). If we now abstract away from that very low-level view, we can see that it could also be viewed as two separate two-digit displays (one pair for the hours and one pair for the minutes). One pair starts at 0, increases by 1 each hour, and rolls back to 0 after reaching its final value of 23\. The other rolls back to 0 after reaching its final value of 59\. The similarity in behavior of these two displays might then lead us to abstract away even further from viewing the hours display and minutes display distinctly. Instead, we might think of them as being objects that can display values from zero up to a maximum. The value can be incremented, but, if the value reaches the maximum, it next rolls over to zero. Now we seem to have reached an appropriate level of abstraction that we can represent as a class: a two-digit display class.

For our clock display, we shall first program a class for a two-digit number display (**Figure 3.2**), then give it an accessor method to get its value, and two mutator methods to set the value and to increment it. Once we have defined this class, we can just create two objects of the class with different limits to construct the entire clock display.

When we discussed fields in [**Chapter 2**](#urn_pearson_manifest_ed82c621-0993-4659-8365-ae64f154e3fe.xhtml), we said that the word “private” in the field declaration is followed by a type and a name for the field. Here we use the class `NumberDisplay` as the type for the fields named `hours` and `minutes`. This shows that class names can be used as types. In effect, every time we write a class, we are adding a new type to the language. That means we can then declare variables to be of our new class type.

The type of a variable specifies what kind of values can be stored in the variable. If the type is a class, then the variable can hold objects of that class. However, declaring a field or other variable of a class type does not automatically create an object of that type; instead, the field is initially empty. In Java we say that an empty variable holds the value `null`. We do not yet have a `NumberDisplay` object. The associated object will have to be created explicitly, and we shall see how this is done when we look at the constructor of the `ClockDisplay` class.

# 3.6: Class diagrams Versus object diagrams

The structure described in the previous section (one `ClockDisplay` object holding two `NumberDisplay` objects) can be visualized in an *object diagram* as shown in **Figure 3.3a**. In this diagram, you see that we are dealing with three objects. **Figure 3.3b** shows the *class diagram* for the same situation.

#### Figure 3.3 **Object diagram and class diagram for the ClockDisplay**

![The figure has two diagrams that depict the number displayed in a clock.](images/9f85839c-0666-4c3a-a30b-66584b854a80_ASSET_FG_03_003.png "View Image")

(a) The diagram shows three boxes to depict the ClockDisplay and its two NumberDisplays. The first box, titled, myDisplay colon ClockDisplay has the following: hours: a blank square box, minutes: a blank square box. The second box, titled, colon NumberDisplay has the following text inside: 11\. The third box, titled, colon NumberDisplay has the following text inside: 03\. An arrow from the blank square box corresponding to hours in the first box runs to the second box. An arrow from the blank square box corresponding to minutes in the first box runs to the third box.

(b) An arrow runs from a box titled ClockDisplay to a box titled NumberDisplay.

Note that the class diagram shows only two classes, whereas the object diagram shows three objects. This has to do with the fact that we can create multiple objects from the same class. Here, we create two `NumberDisplay` objects from the `NumberDisplay` class.

These two diagrams offer different views of the same application. The class diagram shows the *static view*. It depicts what we have at the time of writing the program. We have two classes, and the arrow indicates that the class `ClockDisplay` makes use of the class `NumberDisplay` (`NumberDisplay` is mentioned in the source code of `ClockDisplay`). We also say that `ClockDisplay` *depends on* `NumberDisplay`.

To start the program, we will create an object of class `ClockDisplay`. We will program the clock display so that it automatically creates two `NumberDisplay` objects for itself. Thus, the object diagram shows the situation at *runtime* (when the application is running). This is also called the *dynamic view*.

The object diagram also shows another important detail: when a variable stores an object, the object is not stored in the variable directly, but rather an *object reference* is stored in the variable. In the diagram, the variable is shown as a white box, and the object reference is shown as an arrow. The object referred to is stored outside the referring object, and the object reference links the two.

It is important to understand these two different diagrams and different views. BlueJ displays only the static view. You see the class diagram in its main window. To plan and understand Java programs, you need to be able to construct object diagrams on paper or in your head. When we think about what our program will do, we think about the object structures it creates and how these objects interact. Being able to visualize the object structures is essential.

# 3.7: Primitive types and object types

Java knows two very different kinds of type: *primitive types* and *object types*. Primitive types are all predefined in the Java language. They include `int` and `boolean`. A complete list of primitive types is given in [**Appendix B**](#urn_pearson_manifest_fbb3467e-34e7-4105-983a-773ff2410b32.xhtml). Object types are those defined by classes. Some classes are defined by the standard Java system (such as `String`); others are those classes we write ourselves.

Both primitive types and object types can be used as types, but there are situations in which they behave differently. One difference is how values are stored. As we could see from our diagrams, primitive values are stored directly in a variable (we have written the value directly into the variable box—for example, in [**Chapter 2**](#urn_pearson_manifest_ed82c621-0993-4659-8365-ae64f154e3fe.xhtml), **Figure 2.3**). Objects, on the other hand, are not stored directly in the variable, but instead a reference to the object is stored (drawn as an arrow in our diagrams, as in **Figure 3.3a**).

We will see other differences between primitive types and object types later.

The constructor receives the roll-over limit as a parameter. If, for example, 24 is passed in as the roll-over limit, the display will roll over to 0 at that value. Thus, the range for the display value would be 0 to 23\. This feature allows us to use this class for both hour and minute displays. For the hour display, we will create a `NumberDisplay` with limit 24; for the minute display, we will create one with limit 60. The constructor stores the roll-over limit in a field and sets the current value of the display to 0.

Next follows a simple getter method for the current display value (`getValue`). This allows other objects to read the current value of the display.

The sections after the following exercises discuss some new features that have been used in the `setValue`, `getDisplayValue` and `increment` methods.

## 3.8.1: The logical operators

The mutator method `setValue` is interesting because it does not exactly follow the pattern for setter methods that we described in [**Chapter 2**](#urn_pearson_manifest_ed82c621-0993-4659-8365-ae64f154e3fe.xhtml). Although it does contain an assignment of the parameter, `replacementValue`, to the `value` field, it first makes sure that the `value` field is not being set to a value outside the valid range. It reads:

```
public void setValue(int replacementValue)
{
   if((replacementValue >= 0) && (replacementValue < limit)) {
       value = replacementValue;
   }
}
```

The valid range, as discussed above, is zero to one less than the limit. We use an if-statement to check that the value is legal before we assign it. The symbol “&&” is a logical “and” operator. It causes the condition in the if-statement to be true only if both the conditions on either side of the “&&” symbol are true. See the “Logic operators” note that follows for details. [**Appendix C**](#urn_pearson_manifest_6d1eb3ef-4b9f-41bb-bba5-a8c39c999ddc.xhtml) shows a complete table of logic operators in Java. Note that the replacement value must be strictly less-than the limit value, so a value equal to the limit must be rejected. You will have seen that this was the case in [**Exercise 3.9**](#urn_pearson_manifest_a3b41382-e96e-42b3-9a72-6bbb8c6f069b.xhtml).

## 3.8.2: String concatenation

In [**Chapter 2**](#urn_pearson_manifest_ed82c621-0993-4659-8365-ae64f154e3fe.xhtml), we introduced the concept of string concatenation to print a ticket in the `TicketMachine` class: using the '`+`' operator to create a new string out of a mix of strings and integers. The `getDisplayValue` method uses the same technique but, as its “get” name suggests, it *returns* a String rather than printing one.

In contrast to the `getValue` method, we want to return the value of the `value` field in the form of a two-digit string rather than an integer. The rationale for this method is that, if the current time is 3:05 a.m., the clock display should read 03:05 and not 3:5\. To get the values of the individual `NumberDisplay` objects in this form, the `getDisplayValue` method returns the current integer value as a String, and it adds a leading 0 if the value is less than 10\. Here is the code:

```
public String getDisplayValue()
{
    if(value < 10) {
        return "0" + value;
    }
    else {
        return "" + value;
    }
}
```

Note that the zero ("`0`") is written in double quotes. Thus, we have written the *String* 0, not the *integer number* 0\. Then the expression

```
"0" + value
```

concatenates a String and an integer (because the type of `value` is integer). The plus operator, therefore, represents string concatenation again, as seen in [**Section 2.9**](#urn_pearson_manifest_e3be5454-ce35-4a7f-8d1b-b390f3cb3c2e.xhtml). Before continuing, we will now look at string concatenation a little more closely.

The plus operator (`+`) has different meanings, depending on the type of its operands. If both operands are numbers, it represents addition, as we would expect. Thus,

```
42 + 12
```

adds those two numbers, and the result is 54\. However, if the operands are strings, then the meaning of the plus sign is string concatenation, and the result is a single string that consists of both operands stuck together. For example, the result of the expression

```
"Java" + "with BlueJ"
```

is the single string

```
"Javawith BlueJ"
```

Note that a space is not added between the strings. If you want a space, you must include it yourself within one of the strings.

If one of the operands of a plus operation is a string and the other is not, then the other operand is automatically converted to a string, and then a string concatenation is performed. Thus,

```
"answer: " + 42
```

results in the string

```
"answer: 42"
```

This works for all types. Whatever type is “added” to a string is automatically converted to a string and then concatenated.

Back to our code in the `getDisplayValue` method. If `value` contains 3, for example, then the statement

```
return "0" + value;
```

will return the string `"03"`. In the case where the value is greater than 9, we have used a little trick:

```
return "" + value;
```

Here, we concatenate `value` with an empty string. The result is that the value will be converted to a string and no other characters will be prefixed to it. We are using the plus operator for the sole purpose of forcing a conversion of the integer value to a value of type `String`.

In a later section of this chapter, we shall look at an alternative way to format strings from multiple elements.

In a later section of this chapter, we shall discuss a way to format strings that avoid some of these potential problems.

## 3.8.3: The increment method

The last method in the `NumberDisplay` class increments the display value by 1\. It takes care that the value resets to 0 when the limit is reached:

```
public void increment()
{
    value = value + 1;
    if(value == limit) {
        value = 0;
    }
}
```

The task of rolling over at the limit is implemented slightly differently in the version of `NumberDisplay` that can be found in the full *clock-display* project. That version uses the 'modulo operator' to detect the rollover point and is discussed in [**Section 3.12.3**](#urn_pearson_manifest_686a7b7d-4ede-4a87-aab8-dae8c9549913.xhtml).

# 3.10: Objects creating objects

The first question we have to ask ourselves is: Where do the `NumberDisplay` objects used by the `ClockDisplay` come from? As a *user* of a clock display, when we create a `ClockDisplay` object we assume that our clock display has hours and minutes. So, by simply creating a clock display, we have implicitly created two number displays for the hours and minutes.

However, as *writers* of the `ClockDisplay` class, we must make this happen. To do this, we write code in the constructor of the `ClockDisplay` that creates two `NumberDisplay` objects. Because the constructor is automatically executed when a `ClockDisplay` object is created, the `NumberDisplay` objects will automatically be created at the same time. Here is the code of the `ClockDisplay` constructor that makes this work:

```
public class ClockDisplay
{
    private NumberDisplay hours;
    private NumberDisplay minutes;

    Remaining fields omitted.

    public ClockDisplay()
    {
        hours = new NumberDisplay(24);
        minutes = new NumberDisplay(60);
        updateDisplay();
    }

    Methods omitted.

}
```

Each of the first two lines in the constructor creates a new `NumberDisplay` object and assigns it to a field. The syntax of an operation to create a new object is

```
new ClassName (argument-list)
```

The `new` operation does two things:

1.  It creates a new object of the named class (here, `NumberDisplay`).
2.  It executes the constructor of that class.

If the constructor of the class is defined to have parameters, then the corresponding arguments must be supplied in the `new` statement. For instance, the constructor of class `NumberDisplay` was defined to expect one integer parameter:

```
public NumberDisplay(int rollOverLimit)
```

Thus, the `new` operation for the `NumberDisplay` class, which calls this constructor, must provide one argument of type `int` to match the defined constructor header:

```
new NumberDisplay(24)
```

This parameter passing is the same as for methods discussed in [**Section 2.5**](#urn_pearson_manifest_fcaa54c7-f7da-47b2-9574-24f6b50c18ea.xhtml). With this constructor, we have achieved what we wanted: if someone now creates a `ClockDisplay` object, the `ClockDisplay` constructor will automatically execute and create two `NumberDisplay` objects. From the point of view of a user of the `ClockDisplay` class, the creation of the `NumberDisplay` objects is implicit. However, from a writer’s point of view, the creation is explicit because they must write the code to make it happen.

The final statement in the constructor is a call to `updateDisplay` that sets up the `displayString` field. This call is explained in [**Section 3.12.1**](#urn_pearson_manifest_002abc3c-1fc4-4495-8b1d-2ea77e6e2474.xhtml). Once that method has been run, the clock display is ready to be used.

# 3.11: Multiple constructors

You might have noticed when you created a `ClockDisplay` object that the pop-up menu offered you two ways to do that:

```
new ClockDisplay()
new ClockDisplay(int hour, int minute)
```

This is because the `ClockDisplay` class contains two constructors. What they provide are alternative ways of initializing a `ClockDisplay` object. If the constructor with no parameters is used, then the starting time displayed on the clock will be 00:00\. If, on the other hand, you want to have a different starting time, you can set that up by using the second constructor. It is common for class definitions to contain alternative versions of constructors or methods that provide various ways of achieving a particular task via their distinctive sets of parameters. This is known as *overloading* a constructor or method.

# 3.12: Method calls

## 3.12.1: Internal method calls

The last line of the first `ClockDisplay` constructor is the statement

```
updateDisplay();
```

This statement is a *method call*. As we have seen above, the `ClockDisplay` class has a method with the following header:

```
private void updateDisplay()
```

The method call above invokes this method. Because this method is in the same class as the call of the method, we also call it an *internal method call*. Internal method calls have the syntax

```
methodName ( argument-list )
```

We contrast internal method calls with external method calls in the next section.

In our example, the method does not have any parameters, so the argument list is empty. This is signified by the pair of parentheses with nothing between them.

When a method call is encountered, the matching method is executed, and the execution returns to the method call and continues at the next statement after the call. For a method signature to match the method call, both the name and the parameter list of the method must match. Here, both the parameter list and argument list are empty, so they match. This need to match against both method name and parameter lists is important, because there may be more than one method of the same name in a class—if that method is overloaded.

In our example, the purpose of this method call is to update the display string. After the two number displays have been created, the display string is set to show the time indicated by the number display objects. The implementation of the `updateDisplay` method will be discussed below.

## 3.12.2: External method calls

An external method call means a call by one object of a method belonging to another object. This is at the heart of this chapter’s main theme which is seeing how objects can be combined so that they cooperate to perform a common task. For one object to call another’s methods, the calling object must have a name for the other object. We are now going to see how a `ClockDisplay` object can call methods of the two `NumberDisplay` objects it has created, which are called `minutes` and `hours`.

Here is the `timeTick` method of `ClockDisplay`, which is where most of the interaction is performed:

```
public void timeTick()
{
    minutes.increment();
    if(minutes.getValue() == 0) {
        // It just rolled over!
        hours.increment();
    }
    updateDisplay();
}
```

Were this display connected to a real clock, this method would be called once every 60 seconds by the electronic timer of the clock. For now, we just call it ourselves to test the display.

When the timeTick method is called, it first executes the statement

```
minutes.increment();
```

This statement calls the `increment` method of the `minutes` object. The syntax of an external method call is

```
object . methodName ( argument-list )
```

This syntax is known as *dot notation*. It consists of an object name, a dot, the method name, and argument values for the call. The difference between internal and external method calls is clear—the presence of an object name followed by a dot tells us that the method being called is part of another object.

We know that the call to `increment` on the minutes object will either cause the number of minutes to be increased by 1 or for the number to rollover to zero. If it has rolled over to zero then another hour will have passed, and we will need to increment the value of hours. So, immediately after the call to increment on `minutes`, the `timeTick` method has an if-statement to check whether the hours should also be incremented. The condition in the if-statement calls the `getValue` method of the `minutes` object to see whether it has just rolled over. If `getValue` returns zero, then we know that the minutes just rolled over and we should increment the hours. If the value of the minutes is not zero, then we’re done. We do not have to change the hours in that case. Thus, the if-statement does not need an *else* part.

It is particularly important to note that all the external method calls in `timeTick` require the name of an *object* before the dot and not the name of a class. So, we wrote

```
minutes.getValue()
```

rather than

```
NumberDisplay.getValue()
```

and

```
hours.increment();
```

rather than

```
NumberDisplay.increment();
```

The reasons should be obvious from the fact that we have two different `NumberDisplay` objects on which we could call those methods, but beginner programmers often make the mistake of writing a class name rather than a variable name before the dot. If we do not name an object as part of the method call then the call cannot be dealt with by the object it is intended for. This essential principle was illustrated in [**Exercise 3.10**](#urn_pearson_manifest_a3b41382-e96e-42b3-9a72-6bbb8c6f069b.xhtml). Even if there is only one object of a particular type, we must still name that object rather than its class when calling its methods.

In the `timeTick` method, the `ClockDisplay` object is asking the `NumberDisplay` objects to carry out part of the overall task. In other words, responsibility for the overall time-keeping task is divided up between code in the `ClockDisplay` class and the `NumberDisplay` class. This is a practical illustration of the *divide and conquer* principle we referred to earlier in our discussion of abstraction. This sharing of responsibilities across multiple classes and objects is a theme we shall see repeatedly.

We should now also be able to understand the remaining three methods of the `ClockDisplay` class (see **Code 3.4**). The method `setTime` takes two parameters—the hour and the minute—and sets the clock to the specified time. Looking at the method body, we can see that it does so by calling the `setValue` methods of both number displays. Then it makes an internal call to `updateDisplay` to update the display string accordingly, just as the constructor does.

The `getTime` method is a standard getter—it just returns the current display string. Because we always keep the display string up to date, this is all there is to do.

Finally, the `updateDisplay` method is responsible for updating the display string so that it correctly reflects the time as represented by the two number display objects. It is called every time the time of the clock changes. Once again, it illustrates external method calls. It works by calling the `getDisplayValue` method on each of the `NumberDisplay` objects. These calls return the distinctive values of the separate number displays. The `updateDisplay` method then uses string concatenation to join these two values, separated by a colon.

## 3.12.3: The modulo operator

[**Section 3.8.3**](#urn_pearson_manifest_2e56924d-7b11-483c-9ad0-3e507be01888.xhtml) showed the `increment` method in the `NumberDisplay` class increasing the `value` field by 1 and then testing to see whether it had reached the limit. The following alternative version uses Java's *modulo* operator (`%`) to achieve the same.

```
public void increment()
{
    value = (value + 1) % limit;
}
```

The action of the modulo operator is related to integer division. For example, the result of the division

```
27 / 4
```

can be expressed in integer numbers as

```
result = 6, remainder = 3
```

The modulo operator returns just the remainder of such a division. Thus, the result of the expression (`27 % 4`) would be `3`.

In this version of the increment method, (value + 1) is divided by limit. If the sum is less than the limit then the sum is what remains and that is assigned to the `value` field. But if the sum is equal to limit then there is no remainder after division and zero will be assigned to `value`. Try the following exercises to help you understand how the modulus operator works.

## 3.12.4: Summary of the clock display

It is worth considering the way this example uses abstraction to divide the problem into smaller parts. Looking at the source code of the class `ClockDisplay`, you will notice that we just create `NumberDisplay` objects without being particularly interested in what those objects look like internally. We can then call their methods (`increment`, `getValue`, `getDisplayString`) to make them work for us. At this level, we simply assume that `increment` will correctly increment a display’s value without being concerned with how it does it. For instance, whether it uses the modulo operator or an if-statement is irrelevant as long as it implements the task of incrementing correctly.

In real-world projects, these different classes are often written by different people. You might already have noticed that all these two people have to agree on is what method signatures the class should have and what they should do. Then one person can concentrate on implementing the methods, while the other person can just use them.

The set of methods an object makes available to other objects is called its *interface.* We shall discuss interfaces in much more detail later in this book.

# 3.13: Modularization, abstraction, and object-interaction revisited

We are now going to further explore the major themes of this chapter—modularization, abstraction, and object interaction—within the context of the *midi-player* project. This project makes use of the Musical Interface Digital Interface (MIDI) standard. MIDI allows musical instruments and computers to communicate with each other and for complex pieces of music to be digitally encoded and played. However, for this project, we are going to make use of MIDI without exploring any of its details. That is a further example of abstraction and modularization: people other than us have written classes that fully understand the complexities of the MIDI standard, and how to generate sounds using it, but we do not have to know those details. We can use the work they have already done to write our own programs that use their classes.

The *midi-player* project will allow us to compose very simple tunes out of individual musical notes (A, B, C, etc.) and then play them via pre-written classes that know about MIDI. You will not need to know any music theory to do this, or how MIDI works under the surface.

One of the main purposes of this project is to help you think more deeply about the interactions that you have with the objects you create on the BlueJ object bench, and how your interactive method invocations might be written as Java source code. This will lead us to again look at how objects interact directly with each other rather than via you as an intermediary. In some ways, what we will be doing with this project is like what you experienced with the *figures* and *house* projects in [**Chapter 1**](#urn_pearson_manifest_6a3729e4-61bf-4542-b92a-61331e33b5e4.xhtml), where your original interactions with individual shape objects on the object bench in the *figures* project were then written in the form of the `Picture` class in the *house* project.

## 3.13.1: The midi-player project

Open the *midi-player* project. It consists of three classes: `MidiPlayer`, `SimpleTune,` and `Note`.

The purpose of this project is not to teach you any new Java features. If you were to browse the source code of the classes, you would notice some Java features that we have not yet covered, but the goal is not for you to study or understand them yet. Don’t be overly concerned by those aspects of the source code. Several of those new features will be covered in the next chapter.

## 3.13.2: The `Note` class

Given the features of Java we have covered up to this point, you should easily be able to understand the source code of the `Note` class. This class models the idea of a musical note played for a given length of time, called its *duration* in our project. In a piece of music, notes will be played for different lengths of time, and these give the piece some of its character.^([11](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:327e0c0a-6a78-4a54-8e59-1c4afd088f65)) Each `SimpleTune` object will store multiple `Note` objects that represents the sequence of notes that make up that tune. You have already encountered the idea of grouping multiple objects together in the *lab-classes* project, where a `LabClass` object stores multiple `Student` objects for a course, and we will formally introduce you to object collections in the next chapter.

## 3.13.3: Playing tunes

`MidiPlayer` objects have a `playTune` method that can play a simple tune defined in a `SimpleTune` object. We will try out this feature with the following exercise. For this exercise, you might find it useful to turn on method recording in the BlueJ Terminal window: Select *View* and tick the *Terminal* menu item, then in the Terminal window’s *Options* menu tick *Record method calls*. (You should also ensure that the *Clear screen at method call* option is **not** ticked.)

When a `SimpleTune` object is passed to the `playTune` method of a `MidiPlayer` object, the `MidiPlayer` object interacts with the `SimpleTune` object to retrieve the list of `Note` objects that it stores. The player object then plays each note in turn for its associated duration. How that happens in practice can be found by looking at the source code of the `playTune` method in `MidiPlayer`. At this stage of the book, we would not expect you to understand everything you see there because it involves many Java features that we have not yet discussed. However, one of the things that you might recognize is that the source of that method contains a mix of external method calls (from the `MidiPlayer` object to the `SimpleTune` object) and internal method calls (from the `MidiPlayer` to its own methods). For instance, one of the lines is:

```
int instrument = tune.getInstrument();
```

This calls the `getInstrument` method of the `SimpleTune` object `tune`, and puts the value that is returned into a local integer variable called `instrument`. This is an external method call.

Another line is:

```
addNoteToTrack(noteValue, track, tick, duration);
```

The absence of a variable name and dot before `addNoteToTrack` tells us that this is an internal method call and that `addNoteToTrack` must be defined inside the `MidiPlayer` class rather than the `SimpleTune` class.

## 3.13.4: The BlueJ object bench

One of the distinctive features of BlueJ is its object bench. This allows you to interact with objects directly by inspecting their state and calling methods on them. When you interact with an object on the object bench, in effect, you are simulating what happens all the time internally within a program that is running independent of BlueJ. You can see the equivalent code in the BlueJ Terminal window if you have ‘method recording’ turned on.

The source code we write is designed to achieve a task by having the corresponding program at runtime create new objects for itself and arrange for those objects to interact with each other. As you start to write more sophisticated programs you will find that less and less of the overall task is accomplished by you interacting with the objects you have created on the object bench. Instead, you might create a single object, call one of its methods, and then have no further direct interaction with all the program’s many objects while the program is running. You can explore that in practice by completing the following exercises which will guide you through the process of writing a Java class that will create and play a simple tune. In other words, you will write a program that completes [**Exercise 3.42**](#urn_pearson_manifest_a131d824-f298-4a16-b028-b1233cbc43e0.xhtml) rather than solving it by direct interaction. If you had method recording turned on while completing that exercise, then you will already have seen something very close to the source code that you will be writing, so you might like to repeat that exercise with method recording turned on if you did not do so the first time.

## 3.13.5: Programming the playing of a tune

What you are going to do is create a class that takes over the responsibilities of creating a `MidiPlayer` object, creating a `SimpleTune` object, adding some notes to the `SimpleTune` and then passing it to the `MidiPlayer` to play the tune. In your solution to [**Exercise 3.42**](#urn_pearson_manifest_a131d824-f298-4a16-b028-b1233cbc43e0.xhtml) these are all the things you will have done interactively to complete the exercise.

Try completing the three exercises above on your own first before reading on. Compile your project to check whether everything is correct so far. While the class does not do anything useful so far, it should compile without error.

Once you are finished, you can check your work—your class should now look similar to that shown in **Code 3.5**.

Just take care to make any appropriate adjustments to the variable names in your code as they might be different from the code shown there; for instance, `player` instead of `midiPlay1`.

After completing the *midi-player* exercises you should have a class that involves objects creating objects: `TuneCreator` creates a `MidiPlayer` object and a `SimpleTune` object, for instance. There are also several examples of object interactions/method calls between pairs of objects:

*   The `TuneCreator` object calls the `SimpleTune` object’s `addNote` method several times;
*   The `TuneCreator` object then calls the `MidiPlayer` object’s `playTune` method, passing it the `SimpleTune` object (containing all the added notes) as an argument;
*   The `MidiPlayer` object then calls the `SimpleTune` object’s `getNotes` and `getInstrument` methods.

This example illustrates a point central to object-oriented programming: programs typically operate by objects creating other objects and calling their various methods.

# 3.14: Instance methods

[**Exercise 3.10**](#urn_pearson_manifest_a3b41382-e96e-42b3-9a72-6bbb8c6f069b.xhtml) involved incorrectly trying to call a method on a *class name* rather than a variable name. This did not work—the result was an error message.

This situation is worth discussing further, since there are some situation where we do indeed call a method on a class name. Those special methods are called *static methods*, while the methods we have used so for are *instance methods*. Let us first examine instance methods again.

[**Section 3.12.2**](#urn_pearson_manifest_682a5e30-04e7-4b70-9bad-3bf9b2da7be6.xhtml) explained that, when making an external method call, we normally name the *object* on which the method is to be called and not the class. For instance, if you tried to find the balance of money in a `TicketMachine` like this

```
TicketMachine.getBalance()
```

the compiler error would be:

```
non-static method getBalance cannot be referenced
from a static context
```

because the code is calling `getBalance` on the class name and so does not say which machine’s balance is required. If you tried to show the notes of a tune like this:

```
SimpleTune.showNotes();
```

you would get the same message again, because different `SimpleTune` objects will contain different tunes and the code does not say which particular tune object should show its notes.

In [**Chapter 2**](#urn_pearson_manifest_ed82c621-0993-4659-8365-ae64f154e3fe.xhtml) we introduced the fundamental elements of a Java class: its fields, constructors and methods. In all cases, the methods we wrote were *instance methods*. In other words, calls to those methods were always associated with an object. This is an important concept because each object has a state (stored in its instance fields) which is maintained independently of all other instances of that class. If we call `getBalance` on a `TicketMachine` object then we expect that particular object to return the value of its particular balance field at the time of the call, and not the balance of any other `TicketMachine` object. Different objects of the same class will likely return different values, depending on their current state.

# 3.15: Static methods

Instance methods are sometimes referred to as “non-static methods,” which is the wording used in the error message we saw in the previous section. From those error messages, you will probably realize that there are some methods called “static methods.” Static methods are easily identified because they have the `static` keyword in their header. (We have not yet seen an example of these in our code.) At this stage, we will not have any need to write static methods in our own code (we will do so a bit later, see [**Chapter 6**](#urn_pearson_manifest_5d75092a-6ccb-4eaf-97cc-591761ebaeed.xhtml)), but we may want to use some static methods from the standard library. Understanding the difference is also useful for interpreting error messages like the one above.

The significant feature of a static method is that it is not associated with an object but its defining class. The reason is typically that the method does not need to refer to the state of any particular object, but rather does some abstract calculation which can be done independently from a specific object.

For static methods, we call the method via the name of its class rather than an object:

```
ClassName.methodName(argument-list)
```

The following sections provide some examples of those.

## 3.15.1: The Math.abs Method

The standard Java `Math` class serves as an interesting example because *all* of its methods are static. The class defines no instance fields and so has no instance methods. It serves purely as a container to hold a set of mathematical helper functions, in the form of static methods. A consequence is that it is never necessary or useful to create an instance of the `Math` class. It has, in fact, no public constructor.

The following example illustrates one of the static methods of the `Math` class.

Suppose that we want to print the *absolute value* of an integer variable, which is the positive value of a number regardless of whether or not it was negative. Here is the code we might initially think of writing:

```
if(x >= 0) {
    System.out.println(x);
}
else {
    System.out.println(-x);
}
```

In the case that `x` is positive, we simply print its value, otherwise we print negative `x`. However, the `Math` class defines a static method called `abs` (short for “absolute value”), which does the task for us, and which we can use instead. So, we can replace the if-statement above as follows:

```
System.out.println(Math.abs(x));
```

Note that we are calling the `abs` method on the `Math` *class* and not a `Math` *object*. In contrast to the examples that give a compiler error message, this code compiles because `abs` is defined as a static method, and for these this call is correct.

## 3.15.2: The System.currentTimeMillis method

Another example is `currentTimeMillis` in the `System` class. It returns the current time as the number of milliseconds since 1^(st) January 1970\. As you can imagine, that is a lot of milliseconds (there are 24*60*60*1000 milliseconds in a single day), so the return value of the method is of type `long`, which means it is an integer value with a very large range. The following illustrates how the current time in hours and minutes can be worked out following a call to `currentTimeMillis`:

```
long millis = System.currentTimeMillis();
long seconds = millis / 1000;
long currentMinutes = seconds / 60 % 60;
long currentHours = seconds / (60 * 60) % 24;
```

Once again, we call `currentTimeMillis` directly on the `System` class and not on an instance of the `System` class. Note the use of the modulus operator, which we discussed in [**Section 3.12.3**](#urn_pearson_manifest_686a7b7d-4ede-4a87-aab8-dae8c9549913.xhtml), to ensure that the value of minutes will always be in the range 0 to 59 and hours in the range 0 to 23.

This alternative version of the code above differs in that the variables `currentMinutes` and `currentHours` are of type int rather than long. This 'type conversion' is necessary because the `NumberDisplay` objects store `int` values rather than `long` values and a `long` value cannot be assigned to an `int` variable. To convert the long integer values on the right-hand sides of the assignments into `int` values a *type cast operator* `(int)` has been used. The parentheses around `int` are required as they are part of the cast operator.

```
long millis = System.currentTimeMillis();
long seconds = millis / 1000;
// Use a 'cast' to convert long integers to int.
int currentMinutes = (int) (seconds / 60 % 60);
int currentHours = (int) (seconds / (60 * 60) % 24);
```

The `currentTimeMillis` method can also be used to measure how long a task takes to perform in real time: simply get and store the system time at the beginning and the end of a task, and subtract one value from the other. The result is the number of milliseconds that have elapsed.

## 3.15.3: The String.format method—alternative to concatenation

So far, we have used Java’s string concatenation operator “`+”` to build strings out of multiple elements, such as strings and numbers. Because “`+”`  is used for both addition and concatenation, its use for concatenation can lead to some unintended results. An alternative is to use the static `format` method of the `String` class. This works in a similar way to the `printf` method we introduced in [**Chapter 2**](#urn_pearson_manifest_ed82c621-0993-4659-8365-ae64f154e3fe.xhtml) in that it takes a parameter which is a format string that contains format specifiers (for example, `%s`, `%d`, `%n`) and further argument values to be used in place of the specifiers. For instance

```
public String getStudentDetails()
{
    return String.format("name: %s, ID: %s, credits: %d",
                         name, id, credits);
}
```

would substitute the `String` values of the `name` and `id` variables in place of the `%s` specifiers, and the integer value of `credits` in place of the `%d` specifier, to give a formatted result such as:

```
"name: Alice Lyscoe, ID: 348290, credits: 15"
```

The format specifiers take an optional minimum width, which makes it easier to create neatly formatted output in which each component occupies the same space. For instance:

```
return String.format("name: %15s, ID: %6s, credits: %3d",
                     name, id, credits);
```

formats the name in a minimum of fifteen characters, the ID in six, and the number of credits in three.

# 3.16: Using a debugger

We shall now examine the same concept—objects creating and calling other objects— using a software tool: a *debugger*.

So far in this chapter, we have used the most fundamental technique to analyze a given program: code reading. The ability to read and understand source code is one of the most essential skills for a software developer, and we will need to apply it in every project we work on. However, sometimes it is beneficial to use additional tools to help us gain a deeper understanding about how a program executes, and we shall experiment with this now.

A debugger is a program that lets programmers execute an application one step at a time. It typically provides functions to stop and start a program at selected points in the source code, and to examine the values of variables.

Debuggers vary widely in complexity. Those for professional developers have many functions for sophisticated examination of many facets of an application. BlueJ has a built-in debugger that is much simpler. We can use it to stop our program, step through it one line of code at a time, and examine the values of our variables. Despite the debugger’s simple interface, it will be very useful in giving us a great deal of information.

The following exercises will guide you through an examination of the midi-player project using BlueJ’s debugger.

## 3.16.1: Setting breakpoints

To start our investigation, we set a breakpoint (**Exercise 3.54**) in the `SimpleTune`’s `showNotes` method. A breakpoint is a flag attached to a line of source code that will stop the execution of a method at that point when it is reached. It is represented in the BlueJ editor by highlighting the line in red and showing a small stop sign in the left margin (**Figure 3.5**).

The debugger not only allows us to interrupt the execution of the program so we can inspect the variables, it also lets us step forward slowly.
