```
applyPreviousOperator called
displayValue: 3 leftOperand: 3 previousOperator: at end of apply...
displayValue: 0 leftOperand: 3 previousOperator: + at end of plus
numberPressed called with: 4
displayValue: 4 leftOperand: 3 previousOperator: + at end of number...
equals called
displayValue: 7 leftOperand: 0 previousOperator: + at end of equals
```

Print statements can be very effective in helping us understand programs or locate errors, but there are a number of disadvantages:

*   It is not usually practical to add print statements to every method in a class. So, they are only fully effective if the right methods have been annotated.
*   Adding too many print statements can lead to information overload. A large amount of output can make it difficult to identify what you need to see. Print statements inside loops are a particular source of this problem.
*   Once their purpose has been served, it can be tedious to remove them.
*   There is also the chance that, having removed them, they will be needed again later. It can be very frustrating to have to put them back in again!

## 9.9.1: Turning debugging information on or off

If a class is still under development when print statements are added, we often do not want to see the output every time the class is used. It is best if we can find a way to turn the printing on or off as required. The most common way to achieve this is to add an extra `boolean` debugging field to the class, then make printing dependent upon the value of the field. **Code 9.7** illustrates this idea.

# 9.10: Debuggers

In [**Chapter 3**](#urn_pearson_manifest_f1f273a5-68ce-401e-bd3c-a04f01ca891c.xhtml), we introduced the use of a debugger to understand how an existing application operates and how its objects interact. In a very similar manner, we can use the debugger to track down errors.

The debugger is essentially a software tool that provides support for performing a walkthrough on a segment of code. We typically set a breakpoint at the statement where we want to start our walkthrough and then use the *Step* or *Step Into* functions to do the actual walking.

One advantage is that the debugger automatically takes care of keeping track of every object’s state, and, thus, doing this is quicker and less error prone than doing the same manually. A disadvantage is that debuggers typically do not keep a permanent record of state changes, so it is harder to go back and check the state as it was a few statements earlier.

A debugger typically also gives you information about the *call sequence* (or *stack*) at each point in time. The call sequence shows the name of the method containing the current statement, the name of the method that the current method was called from, and the name of the method that *that* method was called from, and so on. Thus, the call sequence contains a record of all currently active, unfinished methods—similar to what we have done manually during our walkthrough by writing marks next to method-call statements.

In BlueJ, the call sequence is displayed on the left-hand side of the debugger window (**Figure 9.9**). Every method name in that sequence can be selected to inspect the current values of that method’s local variables.

# 9.11: Debugging streams

All of the debugging techniques we have described in this chapter apply equally well when writing code that uses streams. The only nuance is the complexity of a typical statement that involves the use of streams. It would not be uncommon for a single statement to contain three or more operations as part of a pipeline, and the ordering and logical flow between those operations will be critical to the correct outcome of the statement. So, it will often be useful to inspect the state of the stream at intermediate points of the pipeline.

The `peek` method is a stream operation that provides the equivalent of using print statements, as a way to examine the state of a pipeline at various points. It is an intermediate operation that can be inserted at any point within a pipeline. It takes a consumer lambda expression as a parameter, but also passes the elements of its input stream unmodified through to its output stream.

For instance, suppose you are reviewing some reasonably complex code—written by somebody else—in the *animal-monitoring* project. The code is meant to create a list of sightings specific to a particular animal, area, and spotter. They might have written this in a single statement as follows:

```
List<Sighting> result =
   sightingList.stream()
               .filter(aSighting -> 
                       animal == aSighting.getAnimal() &&
                       area == aSighting.getArea() &&
                       spotter == aSighting.getSpotter())
               .collect(Collectors.toList());
```

Imagine that the list produced by this code is always empty, even though you are using test data with sightings that should definitely match. Clearly there must be something wrong with the `filter` operation, but you cannot immediately spot the problem. One of the easiest ways to get to the bottom of this would be to split the single filter operation into three separate filters, and to print out fields of the remaining elements after each filtration step. The following version does this:

```
List<Sighting> result =
   sightingList.stream()
               .filter(aSighting -> 
                       animal == aSighting.getAnimal())
               .peek(aSighting -> 
                     System.out.println(aSighting.getAnimal())
               .filter(aSighting -> 
                       area == aSighting.getArea()
               .peek(aSighting -> 
                     System.out.println(aSighting.getArea())
               .filter(aSighting -> 
                       spotter == aSighting.getSpotter())
               .peek(aSighting -> 
                     System.out.println(aSighting.getDetails())
               .collect(Collectors.toList());
```

From this version you would be quite likely to find that the first filter operation is not passing on any sightings to the next, because the test for string equality has not been made using the `equals` method. Once that has been corrected, the tests could be rerun and eventually the `peek` operations can be removed.

A `peek` operation can also be a convenient way to create a position in the middle of a pipeline sequence for setting a breakpoint for a debugger. In this case, you would be more likely to be interested in the states of the objects rather than having something printed, so a consumer lambda that does nothing would be used as the parameter to `peek`, for instance:

```
peek(aSighting -> { })
```

# 9.12: Choosing a debugging strategy

We have seen that several different debugging and testing strategies exist: written and verbal walkthroughs, use of print statements (either temporary or permanent, with enabling switches), interactive testing using the object bench, writing your own test class, and using a dedicated unit test class.

In practice, we would use different strategies at different times. Walkthroughs, print statements, and interactive testing are useful techniques for initial testing of newly written code, to investigate how a program segment works, or for debugging. Their advantage is that they are quick and easy to use, they work in any programming language, and they are (except for the interactive testing) independent of the environment. Their main disadvantage is that the activities are not easily repeatable. This is okay for debugging, but for testing we need something better: we need a mechanism that allows easy repetition for regression testing. Using unit test classes has the advantage that—once they have been set up—tests can be replayed any number of times.

So, the previous programmer’s way of testing—writing a custom test class—was one step in the right direction, but was flawed. We know now that his problem was that, although their class contained reasonable method calls for testing, it did not include any assertions on the method results, and thus did not detect test failure. Using a dedicated unit test class can solve these problems.

# 9.13: Summary

When writing software, we should anticipate that it will contain logical errors. Therefore, it is essential to consider both testing and debugging to be normal activities within the overall development process. BlueJ is particularly good at supporting interactive unit testing of both methods and classes. We have also looked at some basic techniques for automating the testing process and performing simple debugging.

Writing good JUnit tests for our classes ensures that errors are detected early, and they give a good indication which part of the system an error originates in, making the resulting debugging task much easier.

Terms introduced in this chapter:

1.  **syntax error, logical error, testing, debugging, unit testing, JUnit, positive testing, negative testing, regression testing, manual walkthrough, call sequence**

# Chapter 10 Working in Teams

We are now 10 chapters into this book, and you will have written more and more sophisticated programs. As we grow in our knowledge of Java and programming concepts, our programs not only get more ambitious in functionality, but they also become much larger. At some stage we reach a point when we are not able anymore to do all the work ourselves, but we start to work in teams of programmers. And, as we shall discover, this opens up a whole new set of challenges and techniques to deal with them.

# 10.1: The need to work in teams

Programming is a team sport. In the work you have done so far, you may or may not have experienced this already. Perhaps you worked through this book on your own, and all code so far has been written by yourself. Or perhaps you are studying programming as part of a class, and you have already collaborated on some projects with others. Whichever your experience so far, to become a competent programmer, you must learn to work well in a team.

Programming is often portrayed in popular culture as a kind of “lone wolf” activity. Movies abound in which “hackers” sit in dark, crammed rooms in front of an array of screens, working their magic by typing cryptic lines of code into dark, green-on-black text terminals, making use of esoteric expert knowledge only few possess. Nothing could be further from the truth. The fact that these programmers are all too often portrayed as socially challenged young males with questionable hygiene has not exactly done any favors to our profession, or the challenge to attract a wide, diverse population to programming.

Let’s try to look at the reality.

Programming sometimes requires deep individual intellectual work. You will have experienced this. When you work on a challenging problem, or when you are trying to debug a tricky fault, some of the time we work individually, deep in concentration. But this is only one small part of the whole story.

At other times you will have to work with teams of people, describe ideas, discuss benefits and drawbacks of alternatives, communicate a design or an algorithm, and so on. You will need very strong people skills, including teamwork, communication and other social abilities.

In reality, no program of any real interest is developed by a single person anymore. Those times are long over. If you choose software development as a career path, or even as one element of a wider career, you will work in teams.

You may have a job in a small startup, or in a research team; in that case, you might work on a software system in a team of only a handful of people. Or you might work in a large software development company, such as Google or Microsoft, or at a large bank or insurance company. In that case, you will likely work in a team of dozens or hundreds of people.

Programming, at a professional level, is as much a people-centered, social activity as it is a technical one. Good programmers will have both skill sets, technical and people skills.

In a large team, we need people with particular strength in both. Only then can a large and long-lived project be successful.

# 10.2: Technology for team work

Working in software development teams has several elements: organizational challenges (such as project management), general team work skills (such as communication and presentation skills) and a technical part that allows us to deal with the practical problems of working on the same source code of a single system simultaneously with multiple people and still make the system work.

This chapter introduces and discusses only the technical part. We will discuss *source code repositories* and *version control systems* as a technical solution to deal with the practicalities of working in a team on a single system. We will not discuss the other aspects here, as they include enough material for a whole other book. If you are interested, there are many books available discussing the generic aspects, and books about *software engineering*, which discuss these challenges specifically in the context of software development.

# 10.3: Pair programming

Before getting into the main material of this chapter, we shall briefly discuss one specific form of team work, which is quite different from what we will introduce in the remainder of this chapter: *pair programming*.

Pair programming is a way of two people working together on a single piece of software. It has first been described as part of a programming methodology called *Extreme Programming*, a form of *Agile Programming*, developed by Kent Beck.^([22](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:9ef7a04f-39be-400a-a36c-6a7b88e6f23c))

Pair programming works by two people sitting together in front of a single screen, working jointly on writing code. There are several important rules to make pair programming work as intended:

*   Two people work together, but they use only one machine: one single screen and one keyboard.
*   Both people should be similarly skilled.
*   One person is the *driver*, and the other is the *navigator*. The driver has the keyboard and does the typing. The navigator looks at the same screen, thinks and plans and analyzes, and both are in conversation about the next steps, what to write, how to proceed.
*   The two programmers swap places regularly—perhaps every 30 minutes or so.
*   The key is that they do not work separately on different problems but work jointly on the same problem.

Research has shown that this very regularly leads to better quality code than would be developed by a single programmer. While this process is more work intensive than solo work (as it needs two people), in commercial settings this investment can often be recovered later by having fewer errors and better code quality (and therefore saving on debugging and bug fixing effort).

If you have not tried pair programming yourself, we strongly recommend that you do so for your next programming project. This style of work is also great for learning the subtle details of programming and getting new ideas about techniques, whether you are the one getting inspiration from your partner or the one doing the explaining. Good programmers always learn, and talking about code is one of the best ways to do so.

In terms of teamwork, this process does not encounter the fundamental challenges that arise in larger teams. You should try pair programming first, and it will provide a good learning experience, but it will not prepare you for more general teamwork. First of all, pair programming is limited to two people, while real world teams often number in the hundreds. Secondly, the most fundamental technical problem with team work arises from multiple people modifying the same code base at the same time, and all the possible problems that come from this. In pair programming, because only one person edits at a time, this problem does not occur.

In terms of teamwork, a programming pair essentially acts as a single developer. Thus, we can combine pair programming with team work, but this does not remove the need for technical support for working in larger teams.

# 10.4: Teamwork—the Problem

Let us step back for a moment and discuss why working in teams is a technical challenge.

The problem does not stem solely from the fact that many software systems are large (imagine, for example, working on Microsoft Office, or Google Maps: these systems have been developed by hundreds of people over decades and consist of millions of lines of code). We can address the size and complexity issue by using good abstraction techniques, well-designed and documented classes, and good communication in our team.

The central problem is more basic: How can I develop and test my code when another programmer may need to make changes to the same file? What if I need to test, but another programmer is in the middle of some work, and the system cannot be compiled? What if we need to change the same class, and we interfere with each other’s edits?

## 10.4.1: Ad Hoc solutions

When students start working in teams, they often develop ad hoc processes to organize themselves. Many of these are problematic. Consider the problem: Initially, you worked on your own on a single computer, you used BlueJ or another IDE to edit your code, and all is well. Now, you are given the task to work in a team. The goal is to split up the work, implement part of the system each, and make the whole system work together. Every developer has their own computer with a copy of the project under development (**Figure 10.1**). How do we organize the workflow to make this work?

#### Figure 10.1 **Developing a system with multiple developers**

![A diagram displays four laptops, each with a box above it containing a network of four interconnected boxes. A question mark is shown within the diagram.](images/f1d15226-24c9-4459-a0cd-1cc0bb717d3a_ASSET_FG_10_001-1.png "View Image")

A naïve approach is to agree on who edits which class, and then—when your work is finished—send the source code of the class to the other team members, perhaps by email. The team members then have to copy the new source into their own version of the project and continue from there.

Teams who have tried this inevitably discover that this model breaks down very quickly. Often, different team members make changes in their classes that are not compatible, it gets difficult to keep track of which is the latest version of a class, projects cannot be tested, because they cannot be compiled, because a mistake needs to be fixed in someone else’s class, and so on. In short: this process does not work in the real world. We need a better solution.

## 10.4.2: Shared storage

Our next idea may be to store our project in a shared file system. Instead of having multiple copies of the project on every team member’s computer, we use one central version of the project, and all team members work on the same copy (**Figure 10.2**).

#### Figure 10.2 **Using a shared project on a centrally stored server**

![A diagram shows a C P U connected to four laptops. The C P U has a box containing a network of four interconnected boxes above it.](images/83d11b13-630a-4693-a32c-29b23332e470_ASSET_FG_10_002-1.png "View Image")

This model avoids some problems: Team members do not develop using outdated versions of other programmers’ classes, there is no question about which version of a class is the current one (because there is only one), classes do not have to be sent via email, and do not have to be merged into a project manually. There are, however, other problems that remain or arise because of this setup: If one programmer is in an interim state in their development that cannot be compiled, nobody can compile and test their code. If two developers need to edit the same class, there is danger that they accidentally overwrite each other’s changes. We can also not really track who made which change, so when we need to ask questions to a developer, we don’t know whom to ask. Thus, this idea does not provide a good solution either.

## 10.4.3: A Shared repository with local copies

Our next idea is to combine both the previous models: we use a shared server (which we call a *repository*) and also have local copies of the project on each individual developer’s computer (**Figure 10.3**).

#### Figure 10.3 **A shared repository with local copies**

![A diagram shows a C P U connected to four laptops. The C P U and the four laptops have a box above each, containing a network of four interconnected boxes.](images/41785b53-b12e-41c9-be82-f333b667fdbd_ASSET_FG_10_003-1.png "View Image")

With the right technology, this model can be made to work well. Every programmer has their own copy of the project to work on, so work in progress of another developer does not interfere with their own code. Periodically, when a programmer has finished one piece of work, they copy the changes from their local copy of the project back to the repository.

We still have to work out what happens when multiple programmers edit the same class, and how we keep track of the most recent version of each class. Doing so manually would be difficult, but with the right technology support this can be made to work. In the remainder of this chapter, we will investigate how to use a *version control system* (VCS)—software that enables this process to work well.

# 10.5: Working with a shared repository

When we work in teams, we use a central, shared copy of the project and local copies on each programmer’s computer. We will also use software that helps keep these multiple copies in sync, and supports distributing changes made in an organized, reasonable manner.

## 10.5.1: Terminology

To discuss this process and the relevant software, it helps to introduce some terminology.

*   We call the central space that holds the shared project, accessible by all developers, the ***repository**.*
*   The copy of the project held in the repository is the ***primary version***. Copies on developers’ individual computers are ***working copies***.
*   The action of copying the primary version and creating a new working copy on a developer’s machine is called ***checkout***. We say “*I am checking out the project.*”
*   The action of copying local changes from the working copy back into the primary version is called a ***commit***. We can say “*I committed my changes last night.*”
*   The action of copying recent changes from the repository into our working copy is called an ***update***. We can say “*You should update your copy to see the changes I’ve made.*”
*   The process of integrating changes that are committed by a developer into a class in the repository is called ***merging***. When a class is committed by one developer, it does not simply overwrite the repository version. Instead, the system checks if other developers have also made changes to the same class, and the changes are merged into the same source file, keeping all modifications intact. Merging usually works well as long as two developers do not edit the same lines of code.
*   A situation where two developers make different changes to the same lines of a class, and as a result the changes cannot be automatically merged, is called a ***conflict***.

This terminology will help us describe and discuss the workflow we should use when working with a shared repository.

## 10.5.2: The extended workflow

Let us start investigating how the workflow changes in a team project by first looking at the workflow a programmer typically uses in individual development (**Figure 10.4**).

#### Figure 10.4 **Software development workflow for a single developer**

![A flowchart depicts the workflow in software development with respect to one developer.](images/f1578995-bf48-4956-ac06-4281a2107fdd_ASSET_FG_10_004-1.png "View Image")

The flowchart starts with a box labeled Write some code. An arrow runs downward from the box labeled Write some code to a box labeled Test it. Each arrow runs down from the box labeled Test it to two boxes labeled It Works and Doesn't work. An arrow labeled new feature runs back from the box labeled it works to the box labeled Write some code. An arrow labeled fix it exclamatory mark runs back from the box labeled doesn't work to the box labeled Write some code.

When we work on our own, we typically iterate over two possible cycles: We write some code, and when we think we have completed one task, we test it. As long as we find problems, we go back to the code and improve it. We do this until the tests show that the code works. Once that is done, we pick the next task to implement and do the same again. We repeat this, until the program is complete.

When we work on a team project with a repository and a working copy, we need to integrate synching with the repository into our workflow. A first attempt is shown in **Figure 10.5**. The first cycle is unchanged: Again, we iterate over writing, testing, improving until we have convinced ourselves that our code works. It is important to note that we do not commit our code to the repository while it is faulty. This is especially important when our code does not compile: we should never commit code that does not compile to the repository, since it could break all other developers’ versions once they update. They could then not compile their project to test their own work.

#### Figure 10.5 **First version of a workflow with a central repository**

![A flowchart depicts the first version of a workflow with respect to a central repository.](images/7cec15ed-cf12-4714-ac88-0c2cca8c0a15_ASSET_FG_10_005-1.png "View Image")

The flowchart starts with a box labeled Write some code. An arrow runs downward from the box labeled Write some code to a box labeled Test it. Each arrow runs down from the box labeled Test it to two boxes labeled It Works and Doesn't work. An arrow labeled commit runs from the box labeled it works to a C P U and then an arrow labeled new feature runs back from the C P U to the box labeled Write some code. An arrow labeled fix it exclamatory mark runs back from the box labeled doesn't work to the box labeled Write some code.

Once we have finished a task and the code works again, we can commit it to the repository, and it becomes part of the primary version. Then we are ready to tackle the next task.

This process works in principle. There remains, however, one subtle problem in the form of possible *conflicts*. When multiple developers work in parallel, they will all perform repeated updates and commits in an unpredictable sequence (**Figure 10.6**). Thus, as an individual team member, we cannot assume that the primary version has remained unchanged since we last updated our local copy.

#### Figure 10.6 **Updates and commits in a shared development**

![A diagram depicts the process of updates and commits in an unpredictable sequence.](images/debbf7fd-ee8b-4c4d-9ccd-23fdac705e0c_ASSET_FG_10_006-1.png "View Image")

The diagram shows a C P U connected to four laptops. The C P U and the four laptops have a box above each containing a network of four interconnected boxes. An arrow labeled update runs from the C P U to all four laptops and an arrow labeled commit runs back from the four laptops to the C P U.

This leads to the possibility of two developers changing the same class at the same time. In other words, you may have made changes to a class in your local copy, and another developer has changed the same class, and has already committed their version back to the repository.

If you now commit your version, the version control system will attempt to merge the two sets of changes. It will try to work the lines you have changed into the class that was already changed by someone else. Often, when the two programmers have changed different lines of code, this works well, and the merging action is successful. Both sets of changes are preserved in the primary copy.

It is, however, not guaranteed to work. If both developers changed the same lines of code, and changed them in different ways, the version control system is at an impasse: it has no way of deciding which version is the correct one. (Likely, neither single version will now work.) This cannot be automatically resolved. It is called a *conflict*, and this has to be sorted out by humans: the programmers need to talk to each other and decide what to do.

When a conflict occurs, the version control system marks this in the source code with some error text, so that it can be found and fixed. While the conflict is there, the class will not compile.

We can see how a conflict in the primary version effectively violates Rule #1: we now have a primary version that does not compile, which we wanted to avoid. While we cannot avoid conflicts from happening occasionally, there is a solution to this problem. And it lies in a modified workflow.

The crucial detail is that we should perform an update every time immediately before we commit (**Figure 10.7**). The update will merge any changes from the primary version into our local copy, thereby checking for conflicts as necessary. If we have a conflict, it is now present in our local copy, not in the repository version. Thus, we have time to remove the conflict before committing our changes, making sure that no conflict emerges in the primary version.

#### Figure 10.7 **Improved version of a workflow with a central repository**

![A flowchart depicts the improved version of a workflow with respect to a central repository.](images/48cf971b-9ef5-4c06-8aa7-09881f1dc44e_ASSET_FG_10_007-1.png "View Image")

The flowchart starts with a box labeled Write some code. An arrow runs downward from the box labeled "Write some code" to a box labeled "Test it." Each arrow runs down from the box labeled "Test it" to two boxes labeled "It Works" and "Doesn't work." The box "It works" connects to a box labeled "update" and then "update" connects to a box labeled "remove conflicts" and then "remove conflicts" connects to a box labeled "commit." An arrow runs from the box labeled commit to a C P U, and then an arrow labeled new feature runs back from the C P U to the box labeled Write some code. A dashed arrow from the C P U points to the box labeled update. An arrow labeled "fix it exclamatory mark" runs back from the box labeled "Doesn't work" to the box labeled Write some code.

## 10.5.3: Functionality of a version control system

We have seen, in the discussion above, how a VCS supports our work as a team: it organizes exchanging our source code, keeping a central primary version, merging changes into the project and detecting conflicts.

It has additional functionality to support communication in a team: whenever we commit some code, we are prompted to write a *commit comment* (an explanation of what we have changed and why) and other team members can automatically be notified of the change.

In addition to supporting team work, a VCS also supports *versioning*: it keeps not only the most recent version of the primary copy, but a list of all changes made to the project, in their sequence, and with attribution to the author and the commit comments. Thus, it maintains a history of the project: we can see who has made a change, what they have changed, when and why. This information can be used for *version rollback*: the system is able to recreate any previous state of the system. A developer can, for example, issue a command that effectively says “*Revert our primary version back to the state it was last week on Friday at 10am.*”

In this chapter, we will make use of the team work support functionality of a VCS; we will not discuss versioning in any more detail. It is, however, interesting to note that the versioning functionality is useful quite separately from the teamwork aspect. It can be highly beneficial, if you work on a serious project, to use a VCS even if you are a single developer because of the benefits of versioning and automatic backup.

# 10.6: Teamwork in BlueJ

Several different version control systems are available to use, some of them open source and some commercial. *CVS* and *Subversion* are older VCSs, and their use has now declined. Modern systems include *GIT*, *Mercurial* and *Bazaar*; of these, GIT is currently the most popular one.

BlueJ has support for working with a GIT repository built in. We shall now discuss how we can work with GIT with our BlueJ projects. To do this, we will work, as always, with an example: our *World of Zuul* project from [**Chapter 8**](#urn_pearson_manifest_bbb77ecc-45b8-45de-8fb1-efd5b55e0711.xhtml). (Note that it does not really matter at all for this chapter which specific project you use. Any project that contains multiple classes could be used to familiarize yourself with working with the VCS.)

## 10.6.1: The GIT VCS

As mentioned above, for these exercises we will work with a GIT repository. GIT uses a model that is slightly more involved than the general model of repository systems we have described above (**Figure 10.3**). The main difference is that GIT uses two levels of repositories: a *local repository* and a *remote repository*. The local repository resides on your own machine, whereas the remote repository is on the shared server and holds the primary copy (**Figure 10.8**).

#### Figure 10.8 **The repository setup of the GIT VCS**

![A diagram shows various connections among working copy, local repository, and remote repository depicted by a Laptop and a C P U.](images/7161e2c4-7d00-4ee0-9348-4cec2a43a20e_ASSET_FG_10_008-1.png "View Image")

C P U on the right is labeled GitHub, while the laptop is shown on the left. Three blocks, each containing four interconnected boxes are shown on the upper left, upper middle, and above C P U and are labeled Working copy, local repository, and remote repository, respectively. Arrows labeled pull (update) and fetch from the C P U point to working copy and local repository, respectively. An arrow labeled merge from the local repository points to the working copy. An arrow labeled commit from working copy points to the local repository. An arrow labeled push from local repository points to the C P U.

When you use GIT, you still work directly on your working copy on your local machine. However, when you have completed some changes, there are now two levels of copy-operation: you first copy them to your local repository, and then copy them from there to the primary version in the remote repository.

The idea here is that you commit to your local repository frequently (also your work-in-progress), and copy to the remote repository only after your task is complete. The reason for this more complex setup is flexibility: it allows more fine-grained work with different versions, including version rollback on your own, interim changes before you publish your changes to the remote repository. There are some other advantages when using more advanced functionality which we will not discuss here.

To talk sensibly about the steps involved with this model, we need to understand the terminology that GIT uses for the actions involved in this process:

*   The three copies of the project involved in this model are called ***working copy***, ***local repository***, and ***remote repository***. As before, your work is done on the working copy. The remote repository holds the primary version shared by everyone.
*   Copying from the working copy to the local repository is called a ***commit***. Copying from the local repository to the remote repository is called a ***push***.
*   The reverse, getting changes from the primary version into your working copy is also a two-step process. Copying changes from the remote repository into the local repository is called a ***fetch***, and copying from the local repository into your working copy is a ***merge***.
*   It is, however, rarely useful to do a fetch without also doing a merge. Usually, these two actions are carried out together. The combined operation is called a ***pull*** or ***update***.

In BlueJ, you will see the terms *commit*, *push* and *update* appear in the interface. We do not need to deal with separate fetch/merge operations.

## 10.6.2: GIT repository hosting services

To use GIT, you need a server that is accessible by all team members. It is possible to set up and run a server yourself, but this is much more complex than necessary for most non-professional users. Instead, we will use a free, publicly available GIT host.

Several of these GIT hosting services are available, and they usually have a browser-based web interface to work with them. At time of writing, the most popular ones are *GitHub*, *Bitbucket* and *GitLab*. You can find them easily by doing a web search.

All of these systems have a mixed free/commercial business model: they let you use the base functionality free and charge for some of the more advanced functions. The functionality they offer is very similar. For the purpose of these exercises, we will use GitHub. This, however, is not a value judgement; you could use any of these if the offered functionality or their terms of service suit your needs better.

## 10.6.3: Creating a repository

The first two steps to working with a GIT repository are to sign up to a publicly available GIT hosting service, and to create the repository. Let us do that now.

To create a repository, log in to your GitHub account and choose the “New repository” option from the + menu near the top right of the screen. Fill in the detail you are asked for, including a repository name and description (**Figure 10.9**). Make the project private (otherwise the whole world can see it) and make sure to **uncheck the option to add a README file**. (BlueJ creates its own README file, and this would interfere with this.)

## 10.6.4: Sharing your project

Now that we have created server space for our repository, we need to initialize the repository and copy our project into it. BlueJ can take care of this for us.

First, show BlueJ’s team controls by selecting the small arrow at the bottom of the main window toolbar (**Figure 10.11**).

#### Figure 10.11 **The teamwork section in BlueJ’s toolbar**

Next, we want to enable other team members to gain access to our repository. Since the repository is private, only named collaborators will have access. We can add collaborators by going to the repository via its web interface, and clicking on *Settings* and *Collaborators*.

## 10.6.5: Checkout

Now that Alice has created the repository and added the team members, Bob can get a copy of the project by doing a *checkout*.

To do a checkout, you should use BlueJ, and you do not need to have a project open. The checkout function in BlueJ is in the `Team` submenu in the `Tools` menu.

Once you start a checkout, you will see a dialog similar to the one we used to share the project. Fill in the information with the relevant details, and check that everything is okay using the *Check connection* button before starting the checkout. (You can ignore the *Branch* field. GIT supports working in separate branches to keep different pieces of work separate for a while before merging them back together. This is a more advanced use of GIT which we will not discuss here.)

When you check out a project, you will be asked for a name and place to save it locally. Name the project appropriately, and you are ready to work on the project.

## 10.6.6: Checking the project status

Both Alice and Bob now have a working copy of a shared project, with the primary copy in the remote repository. You will also notice that the *Teamwork* section in BlueJ’s toolbar now shows a number of additional buttons (**Figure 10.12**). These are for the functionality you need to use regularly during teamwork, while less frequently used functions are in the `Team` menu.

## 10.6.7: Working as a team

Alice and Bob are now ready to start work on the shared project. They will agree who does what and each start on their own tasks. Whenever they have finished a subtask to the point where it compiles and makes sense to share with the team, they will use commit commands to share their latest version, and updates to get changes from others.

In BlueJ, since we use GIT mainly for team work and not for versioning, it is rarely useful to do a commit without a push. Normally, we will do both together, as you did here.

You will also have noticed that you were prompted to write a *commit comment* (**Figure 10.13**). It is good practice (and very much expected) that you write a meaningful comment here. (In fact, BlueJ will not allow you to commit without entering something into this field.) We will later see how this can be used to view the history of the project, and see who did what work, and when.

In this dialogue, you also have the option to share the BlueJ diagram layout. Teams may decide whether to share their layout or whether they prefer to maintain individual layout.

An update in BlueJ performs both GIT’s *fetch* and *merge* operations. In some cases, you will be prompted to commit first before making an update. This is needed to support merging if the same class has been modified by both team members. In that case, do as suggested: do a commit first (without the push), and then try the update again.

## 10.6.8: Resolving conflicts

When we introduced the concept of repository-based teamwork, we mentioned the possibility of *conflicts*. These occur when two or more programmers change the same lines in the same class, and as a result the system is unable to merge the changes.

In the previous exercise, you will notice that Alice is prompted to do a commit first. When she does, and you pay close attention, you will notice that BlueJ allows the commit but does not allow a push. This is because BlueJ already notices the resulting conflict and prevents pushing the change into the primary copy.^([24](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:62675d14-f9cd-4696-834a-7b1a6b69d61d))

When a conflict arises, it needs to be resolved by the developers. The system cannot decide automatically which version to choose, or how to merge the changes. It will, instead, show both versions of the altered lines, separated by markers:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
 Lines of code as written by Alice
=======
 Lines of code as written by Bob
>>>>>>> 42ba6890e9ca7d1bea56813cc62b2bc1a34e7793
```

A row of `<<<<<` symbols and the word HEAD mark the start of the conflict, and a row of `>>>>>` symbols and an identifier number mark the end.

The two developers involved must now talk, agree on how to proceed, and then one of them has to fix the conflict by replacing the markers with a single block of code, as agreed by both parties.

In practice, if a team is well organized, conflicts do not occur very frequently. If different team members work on different tasks, chances are that they will edit different sections of the code most of the time, and their versions can be merged without problem.

The chances of conflicts grow when team members work separately for long times. To avoid conflicts, it helps to commit and update frequently. Generally, it is good practice to update and commit/push whenever you have reached a state in your implementation that compiles and works well enough not to hold up other developers.

## 10.6.9: Project history

One last bit of functionality to explore is the project history.

The project history can be used in various different ways. It can be used to find a developer who has made a particular change, in case we need to ask them a question, it can be used to investigate at what time (and why) a particular change was made, and it can be used to summarize which team member did which work on a shared project.

All this will be useful only if team members wrote meaningful commit comments, so being aware of this will help greatly with deciding what (and how much detail) to write with your commits.

# 10.7: More teamwork functionality

BlueJ exposes directly only a subset of functionality provided by GIT. The functionality discussed here is sufficient for the most common tasks of working in a team, and what we have seen illustrates the important principles of teamwork.

Additional functionality is available via the web interface of your GIT repository. Here, you can work with branches to support a longer time of a developer working on a separate copy, to be merged back into the primary version later on, you can set up email notifications to be notified of changes made by other team members in real time, and you can make use of additional functionality, such as issue tracking and a project wiki. Perhaps most importantly, you can also use version rollback to reinstate previous versions of your project if something is irretrievably broken.

These functions are beyond the scope of this book; we encourage you to investigate them in your own time when they become interesting. It is useful, however, to know that you can perfectly well work on a repository through BlueJ and the web interface in parallel.

# 10.8: Summary

In this chapter, we have introduced the main concepts of teamwork based on using a shared repository and a version control system, and we have experimented with the functionality in BlueJ to support these concepts.

The implementation in BlueJ uses GIT as the version control software, as this is by far the most popular system in use today. We have discussed which parts of GIT are directly used by BlueJ, and pointed to additional functionality that readers may like to explore on their own as they continue to work in larger teams.

Conceptually, the teamwork workflow is not especially difficult to understand and apply. To really get used it, however, it is important to use it in practice for a while. We recommend that you tackle one of your next projects in a team, if you have not yet done so, and that you make use of the tools described here.

Teamwork integration is not specific to BlueJ as an IDE. If and when you use another environment for your work, you will see that all modern environments have support for using version control systems.

Terms introduced in this chapter:

**teamwork, pair programming, version control system, VCS, source code repository, primary version, working copy, checkout, commit, push, update, pull, fetch, merge/merging, conflict, versioning, rollback**

# Chapter 11 Recursion

# 11.1: Introduction

In this chapter, we will introduce the important programming and computer science topic of *recursion*. A simple explanation is that recursion provides a way to do things repeatedly, something that we have exclusively used loops for up to this point. In a more general sense, recursion occurs when something is defined by reference to itself. Recursion is a powerful programming feature that applies both to the way that methods are written and the way that the data elements of classes are defined.

Anything that can be programmed iteratively (with a loop) can also be programmed recursively, and vice versa. In fact, some programming languages do not have iterative control structures, such as while loops and for loops, and only have recursion available as the way to achieve the same effects. Such languages typically belong to the family of *functional programming languages*. Both recursion and iteration are available in Java so we will sometimes have the choice to solve a particular task either iteratively or recursively. Which to use in any particular situation will depend on different factors. Some tasks can be expressed more clearly using recursion than iteration. On the other hand, iterative solutions are sometimes more efficient to execute than the equivalent recursive ones.

Recursion also applies to the definition of classes, and it becomes visible in the data elements of a class, such as its fields. This is the case where classes model *recursive data structures*, such as *trees* and *graphs*.

In this chapter, we will discuss both types of recursion: recursive methods and recursive definition of classes. In practice, these often go together: when class definitions are recursive, we will often find that tasks involving them are most easily coded using recursive methods.

# 11.2: Recursive methods

The simplest way to describe a recursive method is that it is a method that calls itself. **Code 11.1** shows an example.

#### Code 11.1 **A recursive method**

![A code depicts the recursive 'hello' method.](images/63f49b2e-409b-4d58-9ba3-4a34bf4f810a_ASSET_Code_11_001.jpg "View Image")

Line 1: ForwardSlash asterisk asterisk

Line 2: Indentation level 1, asterisk Recursive single quote hello single quote method.

Line 3: Indentation level 1, asterisk ForwardSlash

Line 4: public void sayHello OpenParenthesis CloseParenthesis

Line 5: OpenCurlyBracket

Line 6: Indentation level 2, System dot out dot println OpenParenthesis DoubleQuotes Hello exclamation mark DoubleQuotes CloseParenthesis semicolon

Line 7: Indentation level 2, sayHello OpenParenthesis CloseParenthesis semicolon

Line 8: CloseCurlyBracket

Before reading further, you might like to consider what will happen if this method is called.

When the method is called, it prints "Hello!" and then calls itself. That call is what makes this a recursive method. Because the method makes a recursive call to itself, "Hello!" will be printed again, and the method will make another recursive call, and that will go on forever: "Hello!" is printed, the method calls itself; "Hello!" is printed, the method calls itself; again and again.

Hopefully you can see that there is a form of repetition here, even though there is no loop involved. The repetition is the result of the recursive call. The effect is similar to the effect of the following loop:

```
while(true) {
    System.out.println("Hello!");
}
```

This goes on forever printing the string as there is no escape from the loop.

An important point to note about the recursive `sayHello` method is that the very first call to it is never completed because, just before the end of the method, another method call is made—recursively to `sayHello`—and just before the end of that call, etc. None of the multiple calls to `sayHello` ever finishes because there is always another call to be completed before they do.

It would appear that a call to `sayHello` will go on and on printing "Hello!" forever. However, in practice that won’t be the case. The program will eventually stop running as a result of a `StackOverflowError` (**Figure 11.1**).

#### Figure 11.1 **An example of a StackOverflowError**

![A dialog box titled BlueJ: Terminal Window - recursion-experiments illustrates a StackOverFlow Error.](images/c0b94695-6342-47b1-95ec-2a6e1d5bb67a_ASSET_FG_11_001-1.png "View Image")

The dialog box has three colored circles at its top left corner. The top pane shows seven lines, as follows:

Line 2: Hello exclamatory mark.

Line 3: Hello exclamatory mark.

Line 4: Hello exclamatory mark.

Line 7: Hello exclamatory mark.

Line 13: Indentation Level 1, at RecursionTester dot sayHello OpenParenthesis RecursionTester dot java colon 17 CloseParenthesis.

Line 14: Indentation Level 1, at RecursionTester dot sayHello OpenParenthesis RecursionTester dot java colon 18 CloseParenthesis.

Line 15: Indentation Level 1, at RecursionTester dot sayHello OpenParenthesis RecursionTester dot java colon 18 CloseParenthesis.

Line 16: Indentation Level 1, at RecursionTester dot sayHello OpenParenthesis RecursionTester dot java colon 18 CloseParenthesis.

Lines 1, 13, 14, 15, and 16 are highlighted, while all the other lines are disabled.

This is due to the fact that a small amount of memory is used, in an area of memory called the *Stack*, every time a method call is made. Usually, this memory is made available again when the method finishes. In the case of our recursive `sayHello()` method, however, none of our method calls ever finish, because we call the next method before we get to the end. Therefore, we use more and more space, and eventually we will run out of Stack space. The situation of running out of Stack space is called a *Stack overflow*, and this is the error we see here.

Just as we don’t usually want to write loops that never finish (*infinite loops*), we don’t usually want to write recursive methods that never finish. In the following section, we shall see how the *infinite recursion* is avoided.

Infinite recursive method calls usually represent a programming error, just as infinite loops are typically written in error. It is interesting to note the difference in behavior: infinite recursion will eventually “crash” the program with a stack overflow, while infinite loops really can go on forever (and if they do not produce any output, the program seem to “hang”).

## 11.2.1: Avoiding infinite recursion

In order to avoid infinite recursion and the resulting stack overflow, a recursive method needs to include a route through it that does not involve a recursive call. Such a route is known as a *base case*. A base case might involve some non-recursive actions, or it might involve no actions at all. Whether there are actions or not, a base case provides an escape route from the recursion by allowing the end of the method to be reached and the recursion “to unwind.” 

In code, a base case is most often represented by an if-statement, in which one condition includes a recursive call and the opposite condition does not. That is a similar idea to ensuring that there is a route through the body of a while-loop that will eventually cause the loop’s condition to become false and allow the iteration to finish.

Consider the new version of our `sayHello` method shown in **Code 11.2**. This version takes a parameter specifying how many times the message is to be printed.

The most significant difference in this version of the method is that there are now two distinct paths through the body of the method: one is a recursive path and the other is a non-recursive path. Which path is chosen is controlled by the condition of the if-statement. If the value of the parameter is great than zero then "Hello!" is printed and a recursive call is made. If the parameter value is not greater than zero, we have reached the base case, and no further recursive calls are made—the method just finishes.

Notice that in the recursive call the value of the argument passed to the call is one less than that received on the current call. This means that each successive recursive call receives a parameter value that is one less than the value received by its caller. As a consequence, eventually the method will be called with an argument of zero. When that happens, the condition of the if-statement will be false, and the non-recursive route will be taken through the method. That call will then return back to its caller, which will allow its caller to finish and return to its caller, and so on, back to the original call. **Figure 11.2** illustrates what happens when `sayHello` is called with a value of 3 for its `numberOfTimes` parameter.

Notice that every version of the call has its own copy of the `numberOfTimes` parameter, each of which is independent of the others, and each holds a different value received from its caller. At the point where the final call is made, there are four separate versions of the parameter holding the values 3, 2, 1, and 0.

An equivalent iterative version of this method would be:

```
public void sayHello(int numberOfTimes)
{   
    while(numberOfTimes > 0) {
        System.out.println("Hello!");
        numberOfTimes--;
    }   
}   
```

There is only one version of the `numberOfTimes` parameter in the iterative case, and the value it holds is decreased by one on each iteration until it finally reaches zero, when the iteration stops.

With the simplistic examples we have seen so far, it is not clear why a recursive solution would ever be preferable. For this example, in fact, the iteration is simpler and faster. Later in this chapter, however, we will discuss examples where a recursive solution has clear advantages.

## 11.2.2: Divide and conquer

“Divide and conquer” is a problem-solving technique that often involves recursion. The idea of this technique is to take a complex problem and break it into multiple, smaller and less complex problems whose solutions combine together to solve the overall original problem. Those relatively smaller problems will often be further broken down into multiple even smaller problems until the sizes of the remaining problems can be solved relatively easily. This is related to the idea of modularization that we discussed in [**Chapter 3**](#urn_pearson_manifest_f1f273a5-68ce-401e-bd3c-a04f01ca891c.xhtml).

The repeated breaking up of the sub-problems is often achieved recursively, with the lowest-level problems becoming the non-recursive base case that allows the recursion to terminate.

A potentially useful feature of the divide and conquer approach is that the sub problems can often be solved independently and, therefore, in parallel—making good use of multi-core processors. Furthermore, those problems that involve processing a substantial amount of data may also make efficient use of memory caches at the lowest level of the solution as the amount of data involved there is likely to be significantly smaller.

As an example of the divide-and-conquer approach, suppose that we want to find whether a particular object or value occurs within a collection, which could be an array or a list. If the collection is unsorted, then we would need to look at every element in sequence. This search from beginning to end would require (on average) a check of half the items before we find the value if it is in the collection, or a search of the whole collection if it is not. For a large collection, that is a relatively slow approach.

However, we can do better if we have a sorted copy of the collection. With a sorted collection, it is possible to reduce the search time significantly by searching recursively using a *binary search*, which is an example of the divide-and-conquer technique^([25](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:f27a941e-18eb-4b63-8cf0-20f521dc0124)).

The *recursion-experiments* project contains a class named `BinarySearchTester` that illustrates this technique via example code to search an array of integers. It has two constructors (**Code 11.3**). The default constructor (the one without parameters) creates an array of 1,000 randomly generated integer values, sorts them, and then performs two searches using the binary search algorithm implemented in the `Searcher` class: one search of a value that does exist in the data and another search for a value that does not exist.

The second constructor allows you to create a test array of a size of your choice. You can then use the object’s other methods to print out the dataset and perform some searches interactively.

The binary search process makes use of the fact that the values in the collection to be searched are sorted in increasing order. When we search for a value, we start by checking the element in the middle of our collection and comparing it to the search value (or near the middle, if there are an even number of elements). One of three possible cases will always apply:

*   The two values match. In this case, the value has been found and the search can stop.
*   The value to be searched for is larger than the value it is compared with. In this case, there is no need to consider any of the values stored at lower indices than the one compared against, because the sorted nature of the collection means that they will all also be less than the value being searched for. It is only necessary to search in the section of the array with indices greater than the one compared against.
*   The value to be searched for is smaller than the value it is compared with. This is the opposite case to the previous one, and so it is only necessary to search the elements with lower indices than the one compared against.

It can be seen that each time the value does not match the one it is compared against, the amount of the collection left to search is approximately halved—the search task is made smaller. For instance, if we search a collection of 101 items and do not find a match on the first attempt, then the search continues among only 50 of the remaining items because the other 50 are either too large or too small. Similarly, on the next attempt, if we do not find a match, then another 25 items are eliminated, and so on. By applying this process repeatedly to smaller and smaller sections of the collection, either the value is eventually found or there is nothing left of the collection to be searched. Contrast that with a linear search of an unsorted collection in which each mismatch only eliminates a single item in the collection and the rest still have to be checked.

The repetition is achieved by making a recursive call to the `binarySearch` method but with a smaller section of the collection to be searched on each recursive call (**Code 11.4**).

What about the base cases? There are two:

*   The target value is found, and there is no further need for a recursive call.
*   There are no further items to be considered, because all the relevant sections have been searched without success: the target value is not in the collection.

The `binarySearch` method in the `Searcher` class performs a *recursive* *binary search* of a sorted array of integers to see if it contains a particular value. If the value is in the array, then the method returns the index of the value, otherwise it returns –1 to indicate that the value is not present.

Although the whole array is passed into the `binarySearch` method each time, each call only considers a section of the array to determine whether the value is present. The section to be searched is indicated by the parameters called `first` and `last`. It is important to note that the parameter `last` always refers to an index 1 greater than the last element of the section. In other words, the method should not examine element `nums[last]`. The search is for the section from `nums[first]` (inclusive) to `nums[last]` (exclusive). Which means that if `first` and `last` have the same value then the search is complete, and the searched-for item is not in the collection.

The searching is initiated by a call to the `search` method taking as arguments the array of integers and the value to be searched for (**Code 11.5**). Its task is simply to call the method that performs the divide-and-conquer search, passing the array and search value along with two additional arguments that define the bounds of the array to be searched. Note that the value passed in as the last argument of the call to `binarySearch` is the length of the array. That value is 1 greater than the last element of the whole array, so it fits with the convention described above.

The binary search algorithm implemented here (as an example of a divide-and-conquer algorithm) illustrates how recursion can be used to implement some solutions much more easily than using iterative approaches. Implementing this algorithm with iteration instead of recursion gets significantly more complicated and results in code that is much harder to understand and write correctly. If you are really curious, try it out. But be warned: it is much harder than the recursive solution.

# 11.3: Recursive classes

So far, we have discussed the general idea of recursion, and then examined one example of a recursive algorithm that operates on an integer array. Recursion has, however, a particular strength where we operate on data that itself is recursively defined. In object-oriented languages, recursive data structures are defined by recursive classes.

Class definitions can be recursive independent of their methods. A class is recursive if the definition of its fields makes reference to the class itself. In other words: a recursive class has at least one field of its own type.

We have, in fact, already seen this in the form of the `Room` class in the *World of Zuul* project. The original version of the Room class looked like this.

```
public class Room
{
    public String description;
    public Room northExit;
    public Room southExit;
    public Room eastExit;
    public Room westExit;

    ...
}
```

and the improved version looked like this.

```
public class Room
{
    private String description;
    private HashMap<String, Room> exits;

    ...
}
```

Both versions define the `Room` class in terms of fields that involve the `Room` class. This means that the `Room` class is defined recursively. An interesting consequence of this recursive definition is that it would be impossible to initialize the room-related fields via parameters to the constructor of the `Room` class. For instance, suppose we tried to add the following constructor to the “bad” version of the `Room` class:

```
public class Room 
{
    public String description;
    public Room northExit;
    public Room southExit;
    public Room eastExit;
    public Room westExit;

    public Room(String description,
                Room n, Room s, Room e, Room w)
    {
        this.description = description;
        northExit = n;
        southExit = s;
        eastExit = e;
        westExit = w;
    }

    ...
}
```

Before reading further, it would be worth trying to work out why this approach is not viable.

Consider what a call to this constructor for the theater would look like:

```
Room theater = new Room("in a lecture theater",
                        null, null, null, outside);
```

This requires that the `outside` room has already been created so that it can be received as a parameter:

```
Room outside = new Room(
          "outside the main entrance of the university",
          null, lab, theater, pub);
```

But creating the outside room requires that the `lab`, `pub`, and `theater` rooms have already been created, because they are linked together. So, we cannot create the `theater` until `outside` is created and we cannot create `outside` until the `theater` is created; they are mutually dependent because of the recursive nature of the class. The same interdependence is present for `outside` and `lab` and `outside` and `pub`. That is precisely the reason why initialization of the exits for all of the room objects is a two-stage process in the Zuul projects: all of the room objects were created with no links to other rooms, and then the `setExits` method was called to make the links.

However, despite this apparent problem, classes with recursively defined data are important for modeling common data structures such as *trees* and *graphs* and we shall return to the recursively defined `Room` class in future examples.

# 11.4: Recursive data structures

The term *recursive data structure* is commonly applied to ways of organizing large amounts of data organized into structured forms such as *linked lists*, *trees*, and *graphs*. The term *data structure* relates to the organization and manipulation of the associated data in languages that are not object-oriented. In other words, languages in which data and the code that operates on it are not explicitly grouped together in a class definition. In such languages, recursive data structures are often implemented as a combination of arrays and “pointers” to dynamically allocated memory, along with recursive “functions” (which are similar to methods) operating on the data.

Object-orientation allows us to unite, in the form of a class definition, data with the functionality that operates on it. A class definition means that the implementation details can be kept private and access to the data is provided via public methods. All of which fits with our goal of encapsulation.

In object-oriented terms, a recursive data structure is implemented by a class that is defined recursively. Although the example of the `Room` class does not exactly fit the mold of one of the classical data structures mentioned above, it does actually have quite a strong resemblance to the concept of a *graph*, which we will examine in more detail later in this chapter.

# 11.5: The file-system project

A good example of a real-life recursive structure is a computer’s file system. Different operating systems use the words *folder* or *directory* for parts of the file system that contain either data files (such as program source files, images, audio files, written documents, etc.) or other folders (directories) that also contain data files and folders, and so on.

We tend to think of file systems as being hierarchical, with a topmost level or “root” (such as a whole disk drive) and files and folders nested within it, each folder potentially having other files and folders nested within it, and so on, until we reach the lowest levels that contain only files and no further folders. Some folders might be deeply nested, with many levels, while others might only be a single level. **Figure 11.3** illustrates a small file system with a few levels of folders and ordinary files.

#### Figure 11.3 **A file system structure consisting of files and folders**

![A diagram depicts a file structure.](images/07ddf522-3d80-4fc5-8958-3626eb184a2b_ASSET_FG_11_003-1.png "View Image")

The diagram shows a folder at the top on level 1\. The folder consists of three files and two folders on level 2\. The first folder on level 2 consists of a folder and two files on level 3\. The second folder on level 2 consists of a file and a folder on level 3\. The first folder on level 3 consists of two files and a folder on level 4.

Since folders can contain folders, they are an example of a recursive structure.

Historically, we call a structure like this a “tree” because it looks a little like an upside-down tree, with a “root” at the top and “branches” growing downward to the “leaves” at the bottom. A leaf is any part of the tree that does not have a further level below it. In terms of a file system, the individual data files would be the leaves, while the folders would have branches growing out of them connected to the data files and folders nested within them. Of course, a folder might be empty, in which case it would be considered to be a leaf.

The *file-system* project is a small demonstration of code working on files and folders in a file system. In Java, a folder is considered to be a special case of a file: it is a file that happens to hold references to other files. Since the `File` class in Java includes folders among its instances, and thus can contain other files, it is a recursive class, and the `File` objects representing our file system form a recursive data structure.^([26](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:62a7533e-9cf0-412e-8ce5-f98e02f92b25)) By experimenting with code that operates on our file system (or at least a part of it), we will see how recursive methods provide an elegant solution to process recursive data.

A typical thing we might want to do with a file system is to find all the files of a particular type. For example, find all the audio files so that we can add them to a playlist. Another example would be to find all the files that are very large so that we can consider them for deletion to free up some space, or to find all those files that contain no data, or all folders that contain no files, so that they can be removed as part of a decluttering process. It can also be useful to add up the sizes of all files contained—recursively—in a folder, so that we can show how much disk space a folder occupies. Each of these functions can be implemented using recursive methods.

We now wish to modify this method so that it lists *all* files contained in our folder, directly or indirectly.

## 11.5.1: Recursive listing of files

Java’s `File` class has a method called `isDirectory()` that lets us check whether a given file object is, in fact, a folder. We have used this method in our `listFolder` implementation (**Code 11.6**) to make sure that we do not attempt to list files that are not folders.

We can now use the same method again to list folders recursively: For each file name we find within our folder, we can check whether that file is, in fact, a folder itself, and if it is, we can recursively call the `listFolder` method on it.

From the exercise above, your for-each loop should now look similar to this:

```
for(File file : folder.listFiles()) {
    System.out.println(file.getName());
    if(file.isDirectory()) {
        listFolder(file);
    }
}
```

When you execute the method, you will have seen that it now lists all files contained—directly or indirectly—in the top-level folder provided. Thus, one simple recursive call has enabled us to process a whole, arbitrarily large recursive data structure, and the code we had to write is quite straight forward to write and understand.

This example demonstrates the real power of recursive methods: when we process recursive data, recursive methods result in code significantly more elegant and easier to write than iterative solutions.

We are, however, not quite finished yet. If our task was to add up the sizes of the files, then this structure would be perfectly fine, since the order does not matter, and we would be finished. For printing, however, the order matters. The format of the output is not ideal (for example, we cannot see which folder a file is contained in in our output), and it will be interesting to spend some time improving the formatting.

## 11.5.2: Improving the format of the listing

A first version of improving our output format is to list our folder contents separately from the filenames.

An observation worth making is that the order of the output we currently see is the result of deciding to print the contents of a sub-folder as soon as it is identified as a folder. An alternative approach would be first to print the full contents of a single level of a folder and only then make the recursive call to print the contents of any sub-folders. In other words, when a sub-folder is identified, it is added to a list rather than being immediately the subject of a recursive call. Only once the current folder’s contents have all been listed is the list of sub-folders iterated over via recursive calls to `listFolder`. **Code 11.7** shows this approach.

# 11.6: Working with recursive classes

In [**Section 11.4**](#urn_pearson_manifest_d195d4bb-d6b4-4e38-86f3-b99c451f1f72.xhtml) we mentioned that recursive class definitions are common in areas that model recursive data structures known as “trees” and “graphs” and that working with such data structures often involves the use of recursive methods.

The connected rooms in the World of Zuul projects are similar in nature to a “graph” data structure, which typically involves an interconnected network of “nodes,” such as you might find in a Metro transport network. We will use a variation of the familiar *zuul-better* project to illustrate some of the ways in which recursion occurs in both the definition of a class and its methods.

The *zuul-recursion* set of projects are similar to the basic *zuul-better* project but the map has a more extensive set of interconnected rooms (**Figure 11.5**). Each room has a name as well as a description, and a “rooms” command has been added to print a list of the rooms’ names:

```
Rooms: outside entrance living-room kitchen garden study
games-room extension landing band-room1 band-room2
```

## 11.6.1: Finding a route

If a player has a map of the rooms, then they can use it to find a route from their current room to another. Route finding using a map is a common task in everyday life and algorithms have been developed to find routes that either minimize the *distance* to be traveled to a destination, or the *traveling time* to arrive at a destination. Such algorithms often involve the use of recursion, and we can use this version of Zuul to illustrate some of what is involved in such a processes.

In the project *zuul-recursion-v1*, the `Game` class already recognizes the command 'route' in order to find the series of moves needed to get from the current room to a destination room. The `Game` class’s `findRoute` method calls the `findRoute` method on the current room object and passes the destination room name as the argument. However, this version of the `findRoute` method in the `Room` class simply checks to see whether the destination room is directly connected to the `Room` object on which it has been called (**Code 11.9**).

Before reading further, take a moment to consider why this attempt will often result in a failure that is the result of infinite recursion and a stack overflow.

The problem with the recursive versions of the `findRoute` method considered so far is that they do not take account of the fact that there is no point revisiting a room that has already been visited. As a consequence, it is possible to become stuck infinitely going backward and forward between a pair of rooms, or going around in a circuit that does not include the target room.

In order to break these cycles, it is necessary to keep a record of those rooms that have already been visited and only recursively call the `findRoute` method on those that have not. **Code 11.11** shows the starting point for this approach, which you can find in *zuul-recursion-v3*.
