The project *imageviewer0-3* provides an implementation of the functionality discussed so far. Open this project and compare it to your own implementation. You will notice a few additional small improvements we have made in this version:

*   We have used a constant called `VERSION` for the version string. This makes it easier to change the version number later. In general, it is good practice to use constants instead of string literals within your code and define the strings as constants at the top of your class.
*   We have implemented the `quitAction` method to actually quit the application. Have a look how this is done. Look up the library documentation for any classes and methods involved.
*   We now show a message that no image has been loaded when the program first starts up. The implementation is simple: we just show an image that states that no (other) image has been selected. This image file is included in the project with the filename *emptyImage.png*.

## 17.7.4: Summary of key GUI elements

At the beginning of this chapter, we listed the three areas of GUI construction: components, layout, and event handling. We have now seen examples of each of these: we have encountered a small number of components (labels, buttons, menus, menu items), we have discussed the principles of arranging the layout of these components, and we have investigated the handling of action events.

Getting to the current state (showing a window with some labels and a few menus) was hard work, and we had to discuss a lot of background concepts. It gets easier from now on—really! Understanding the layout and event handling were probably the most difficult details we had to master for our example.

Adding more menus, other components and improving the layout will now be quite easy—just more of the same. There are a lot of details we may need to look up (such as the exact names and functionality of controls and layout panes), but the fundamental concepts are all the same.

# 17.8: ImageViewer 1.0: The first complete version

We shall now work on creating the first complete version of the image viewer—one that can really accomplish the main task: display and manipulate some images chosen by the user.

## 17.8.1: Image-handling classes

On the way to the solution, we shall investigate one more interim version: *imageviewer0-4*. Its class structure is shown in **Figure 17.15**.

#### Figure 17.15 **The class structure of the image viewer application**

![The figure illustrates a flowchart containing three boxes.](images/7f98a750-7410-4a20-a308-55fa623e7a9a_ASSET_FG_17_015-1.png "View Image")

Each box in the diagram is divided into two parts. The top-left box is labeled ImageViewer in its upper part. This box emits two arrows pointing to other boxes. The first arrow, pointing to the right, leads to the second box, labeled ImageFileManager in its upper part. The second arrow, pointing to the mid-bottom, connects to the third box, labeled "OFImage" in its upper part. An arrow from the box labeled ImageFileManager points to the box labeled "OFImage."

As you can see, we have added two new classes: `OFImage` and `ImageFileManager`. `OFImage` is a class to represent an image that we want to display and manipulate. `ImageFileManager` is a helper class that provides static methods to read an image file (in JPEG or PNG format) from disk and return it in `OFImage` format, then save the `OFImage` back to disk.

For this project, we can treat these classes like library classes; you will not need to modify them.

We shall briefly discuss the most important aspects of these two classes. We shall not, however, explain them completely—that is left as an investigation for the curious reader.

The `OFImage` class is our own custom format for representing an image in memory. You can think of an `OFImage` as a two-dimensional array of pixels. Each of the pixels can have a color. We use the standard class `Color` (from package `javafx.scene.paint.Color`) to represent each pixel’s color. (Have a look at the documentation of class `Color` as well; we shall need it later.)

`OFImage` is implemented as a subclass of the JavaFX standard class `WritableImage` (from package `javafx.scene.image`). `WritableImage` gives us most of the functionality we want (it also represents an image as a two-dimensional array), but it does not have methods to directly set or get a pixel (it uses a different method with an interim class for this, which we want to simplify). So, we made our own subclass that adds these two methods.

The most important methods from `OFImage` for us are:

*   `getPixel` and `setPixel` to read and modify single pixels;
*   `getHeightAsInt` and `getWidthAsInt` to find out the image’s size. (The original `WritableImage` returns its width and height as type `double`, so we have added these two methods, since we will need the values as integers later on.)

The `ImageFileManager` class offers three methods: two to read a named image file from disk (with different parameter types) and return it as an `OFImage`, and one to write an `OFImage` file to disk. The methods can read files in the standard JPEG and PNG formats, and the `save` method will write files in JPEG format.

The additions we made to our class are as follows:

*   We have added a constructor for our class and in it we instantiate an object of type `FileChooser`. `FileChooser` is a standard JavaFX class to show a file chooser dialog. The dialog is initially hidden—it does not become visible on screen at this point. But we have the object ready to show when we need it. We also configure the file chooser so that it starts in the project directory when shown, and we declare an instance variable to store the object for later use.
*   We have now modified the `openAction` method to show the file chooser open dialog, which lets the user select a file to open. If this dialog is cancelled, it will return `null`. In this case, there is nothing further to do. Otherwise, we call `openFile` to open and display the image file.
*   We have added a new method `openFile` to actually open and display an image file. We attempt to load the image, using our `ImageFileManager` helper class. This method will return `null` if the file selected is not a valid image file, so we have to check for this. If the image was successfully loaded (it is not `null`), then we show it on our image label. Finally, we call the `sizeToScene` method of the `stage`. This is necessary because the new image is likely of a different size, and we need to tell our stage that it should resize itself to fit the current scene.

We have also added an import statement for the `File` class.

With this version, we have solved the central task; we can now open an image file from disk and display it on screen. Before we call our project “version 1.0”, however, and thus declare it finished for the first time, we want to add a few more improvements.

*   We want to make our two text labels work: one should display the image filename at the top, and the other a status message at the bottom.
*   We want to add a *Filter* menu that contains some filters that change the image’s appearance.
*   We want to implement the *About ImageViewer* item in the *Help* menu. Selecting this menu item should display a dialog with the application’s name, version number, and author information.

## 17.8.3: Image filters

Next, we shall add some filters to implement some special effects.

The image filters are the first step toward image manipulation. Eventually, we want not only to be able to open and display images, but also to be able to manipulate them and save them back to disk.

Here, we start by adding three simple filters. A filter is a function that is applied to the whole image. (It could, of course, be modified to be applied to a part of an image, but we are not doing that just yet.)

The three filters are named *darker*, *lighter*, and *threshold.* *Darker* makes the whole image darker, and *lighter* makes it lighter. The threshold filter turns the image into a grayscale picture with only a few preset shades of gray. We have chosen a three-level threshold. This means we shall use three colors: black, white, and medium-gray. All pixels that are in the upper-third value range for brightness will be turned white, all that are in the lower third will be turned black, and the middle third will be gray.

To achieve the addition of filters, we have to do two things:

*   create menu items for each filter with an associated menu listener; and
*   implement the actual filter operation.

First the menus. There is nothing really new in this. It is just more of the same menu-creation code that we already wrote for our existing menus. We need to add the following parts:

*   We create a new menu (class `Menu`) named *Filter* and add it to the menu bar (before the *Help* menu).
*   We create three menu items (class `MenuItem`) named *Darker*, *Lighter*, and *Threshold*, and add them to our filter menu.
*   To each menu item we add an action listener, using method references as we discussed for the other menu items. The action listener methods should be called `makeDarker`, `makeLighter`, and `threshold`, respectively.

After we have added the menus and created the (initially empty) methods to handle the filter functions, we need to implement each filter.

The simplest kinds of filter involve iterating over the image and making a change of some sort to the color of each pixel. A pattern for this process is shown in **Code 17.5**. More-complicated filters might use the values of neighboring pixels to adjust a pixel’s value.

The filter function itself operates on the image, so following responsibility-driven design guidelines, it should be implemented in the `OFImage` class. On the other hand, handling the menu invocation also includes some GUI-related code (for instance, we have to check whether an image is open at all when we invoke the filter), and this belongs in the `ImageViewer` class.

## 17.8.4: Dialogs

Our last task for this version is to implement the *About ImageViewer* . . . item in the *Help* menu. When this item is selected, a dialog should pop up that displays some short information.

We do this by adding a listener method named `showAbout` whose job it is to pop up an “About” dialog.

One of the main characteristics of a dialog is whether or not it is *modal*. A modal dialog blocks all interaction with other parts of the application until the dialog has been closed. It forces the user to deal with the dialog first. Non-modal dialogs allow interaction in other application windows while the dialogs are visible.

JavaFX has some special purpose dialogs, such as the `FileChooser` dialog that we have already used, and classes for generic dialog types. For general dialogs, there is a very flexible `Dialog` class that allows us to design and format the dialog in any way we see fit. For easier use, however, there is also a subclass called `Alert`, which provides an easy way to display dialogs in a standard format. For our purposes, this class does all we need, and since it is simpler to work with, this is what we shall use.

When we display an alert, we can specify the type of the alert. The type determines the appearance and the number of buttons. In its default implementation, the appearance varies only in the choice of an icon displayed in the dialog, and the buttons displayed are either a single OK button or an OK/Cancel button pair. **Figure 17.16** shows an example of a simple alert dialog with the alert type set to *INFORMATION*.

Within the box, there is a symbol with a lowercase 'i' inside the circle on the left and the text "ImageViewer Version 1.0" next to the symbol. At the bottom left corner, there is a button labeled "OK."

There is another situation in our program where we should show a dialog. Currently, when we try to open an image file and the user chooses an invalid file (a file that is not an image), we just quietly do nothing (see the implementation in our `openFile` method). This is not good practice; it may leave the user confused about what happened and why no image was loaded.

We should extend our code so that it shows a message to the user, informing them that the file could not be loaded because it was not a valid image file. Add this to your program.

This was the last task to be done to complete “version 1.0” of our image viewer application. If you have done all the exercises, you should now have a version of the project that can open images, apply filters, display status messages, and display a dialog.

The *imageviewer1-0* project, included in the book projects, contains an implementation of all the functionality discussed thus far. You should carefully study this project and compare it with your own solutions.

# 17.9: ImageViewer 2.0: Improving program structure

Version 1.0 of our application has a useable GUI and can display images. It can also apply three basic filters.

The next obvious idea for an improvement of our application is to add some more interesting filters. Before we rush in and do it, however, let us think about what this involves.

With the current structure of filters, we have to do three things for each filter:

1.  add a menu item
2.  add a method to handle the menu activation in `ImageViewer`
3.  add an implementation of the filter in `OFImage`

Numbers 1 and 3 are unavoidable—we need a menu item and a filter implementation. But number 2 looks suspicious. If we look at these methods in the `ImageViewer` class (**Code 17.9** shows two of them as an example), this looks a lot like code duplication. These methods are essentially the same (except for some small details), and for each new filter, we have to add another one of these methods.

#### Code 17.9 **Two of the filter-handling methods from ImageViewer**

As we know, code duplication is a sign of bad design and should be avoided. We deal with it by refactoring our code. We want to find a design that lets us add new filters without having to add a new dispatch method for the filter every time.

To achieve what we want, we need to avoid hard-coding every filter-method name (`lighter`, `threshold`, etc.) into our `ImageViewer` class. Instead, we shall use a collection of filters and then write a single filter-invocation method that finds and invokes the right filter. This will be similar in style to the introduction of an `act` method when decoupling the simulator from individual actor types in the *foxes-and-rabbits* project in [**Chapter 14**](#urn_pearson_manifest_edb2a183-1e4c-4d1d-a85c-a8c7e1f0ad34.xhtml).

In order to do this, filters must themselves become objects, rather than just method names. If we want to store them in a common collection, then all filters will need a common superclass, which we name `Filter` and give an `apply` method (**Figure 17.17** shows the structure, **Code 17.10** shows the source code).

The *imageviewer2-0* project includes a complete implementation of these changes.

In this section, we have done pure refactoring. We have not changed the functionality of the application at all, but have worked exclusively at improving the implementation structure so that future changes become easier.

Now, after finishing the refactoring, we should test that all existing functionality still works as expected. In all development projects, we need phases like this. We do not always make perfect design decisions at the start, and applications grow and requirements change. Even though our main task in this chapter is to work with GUIs, we needed to step back and refactor our code before proceeding. This work will pay off in the long run by making all further changes easier.

Sometimes it is tempting to leave structures as they are, even though we recognize that they are not good. Putting up with a bit of code duplication may be easier in the short term than doing careful refactoring. One can get away with that for a short while, but for projects that are intended to survive for a longer time, this is bound to create problems. As a general rule: Take the time; keep your code clean!

Now that we have done this, we are ready to add some more filters.

Once you have implemented some more filters of your own, you should change the version number of your project to “version 2.1”.

# 17.10: ImageViewer 3.0: More interface improvements

Before we leave the image viewer project behind us, we want to add a few last improvements, and in the process look at two more aspects: buttons and how to use styling to improve the look.

## 17.10.1: Buttons

We now want to add functionality to the image viewer to change the size of the image. We do this by providing two functions: *larger*, which doubles the image size, and *smaller*, which halves the size. (To be exact, we double or halve both the width and the height, not the area.)

One way to do this is to implement filters for these tasks. But we decide against it. So far, filters never change the image size, and we want to leave it like that. Instead, we introduce a toolbar on the left side of our frame with two buttons in it labeled *Larger* and *Smaller* (**Figure 17.2** at the beginning of this chapter already showed these buttons). This also gives us a chance to have a look at fine-tuning layout.

So far, the main part of our window (the area below the menu bar) uses a `BorderPane`, where the left and right areas are empty. We can use the left side of this to add our toolbar buttons. There is one small problem, though. Each area of a `BorderPane` can hold only one component, but we have two buttons.

The solution is simple. We place the two buttons into a `VBox`, and then we add the `VBox` to the `BorderPane`’s left area. **Code 17.14** shows the code to do this.

When we try this out, we see that it mostly works, but does not look quite as expected. Compared to the screenshot shown in **Figure 17.2**, we notice two differences:

*   There is no spacing between the various components, making them all look crammed together.
*   The two toolbar buttons do not have the same width, which makes the toolbar look untidy.

We will fix those two issues in the next two sections, starting with the size of the buttons. But before we do this, let us make the buttons work.

## 17.10.2: Size of components

The size of a component when it is displayed on screen is typically decided by a negotiation between the component itself and the layout pane it is held in. Each component has a preferred size, a minimum size and a maximum size. Containers use these three values to decide how big to make a component. In doing so, they may—or may not—honor the wishes of the component.

A text label, for example, prefers to size itself to be just large enough to display its text. That is, it sets all three of its properties—minimum, maximum, and preferred size—to the same value. A button behaves in a similar manner, but adds a bit of space for some padding and a border. By setting all three size properties to the same value, the button is effectively saying, “I would really like to be this size”.

Most layout panes will try to honor these preferences, and give the button the space it wants. This, however, will not always work. If a user makes the whole window smaller, for example, the layout pane may not have enough space for a component. We have seen in our experiments with layout panes in [**Section 17.6**](#urn_pearson_manifest_270df5b0-e778-4310-b07e-fc0291d6660d.xhtml) what can happen: if there is not enough space, a layout pane may squeeze a button down even below its declared minimum size.

The layout pane itself also has a role: some layout panes have strong views about the sizes of their children and will override their preferences. Or they may honor them if the component has a strong view, and make their own decisions if the component does not care.

In the case of our toolbar, we have a `VBox` and two buttons. The `VBox` would prefer to make all components the same width, but the buttons have a declared minimum, preferred and maximum width. In that situation, the `VBox` yields to the button’s wishes and uses its preferred size.

We can change this effect by changing the button’s properties:

```
largerButton.setMaxWidth(Double.MAX_VALUE);
```

`Double.MAX_VALUE` is a constant in the `Double` class that holds the largest possible value that can be stored in a variable of type `double`. By setting the maximum width for this button to the largest possible number, we are essentially saying *“We don’t have a maximum—make this as wide as you want”*.

Once we do this, the `VBox` effectively decides “*If you don’t mind being wider, then I’ll make you the same width as the pane overall*”.

With this, the base functionality of our image viewer is complete. The last step missing now is styling: arranging fonts, colors and spacing between components to make the interface look nicer. We shall discuss this in the next section.

## 17.10.3: Styling with CSS

So far, we have worked on the functionality of our program, the presentation of the functional components on screen and their relative placement. What we have not done is polish its appearance.

The appearance of our interface is influenced by many different aspects: fonts, font sizes, foreground and background colors, spacing between components, and many other things. JavaFX components have many properties that determine the exact look, and each of these properties can be changed to achieve a different appearance.

The classes that implement each component have methods to change any of these properties, so the natural thing to do seems to be to use these API methods to set the appearance during the construction of our GUI. This would work. However, we shall not do this because there is a better alternative.

JavaFX has a different, more flexible mechanism to define the styling of our interface. Component properties can be defined in a separate file of type CSS (*Cascading Style Sheet*). CSS files were originally invented to style web pages (where HTML files define the content), and JavaFX uses the same mechanism here. Our Java code defines the content of our interface, and a CSS file will add the styling.

In BlueJ, you can create a CSS file using the diagram’s context menu (**Figure 17.18**) or the main menu. CSS files are included in the class diagram, and can be edited directly within BlueJ.

#### Figure 17.18 **Adding a CSS stylesheet to the project**

The CSS file is a simple text file, and it is initially completely empty. Before we can start to write our style rules in that file, we need to do one more thing: we have to tell our program to read the CSS file. We do this by adding our file to the scene’s style sheets, immediately after creating the `Scene` object:

```
Scene scene = new Scene(root);
scene.getStylesheets().add("mystyle.css");
```

Of course, you have to use here the name of the CSS file you chose when you created the file. Now, we can do our styling in the CSS file instead of writing Java code.

## 17.10.4: Using style classes

We are now ready to write some styling rules. Try, for example, the following text in your style sheet:

```
.button {
    -fx-font-size: 20px;
    -fx-padding: 16;
}
```

Write this text into your style file, make sure it is saved, and then run your program again. You should notice the change: the buttons now have a different look.

One interesting aspect of this mechanism is that the code does not need to be recompiled to make changes to the style. Simply editing the style sheet and restarting the application is sufficient. This is one of the great advantages of separate style sheets: since styling often requires detailed experimentation with exact property values, this is much quicker if the program does not need to be recompiled every time. In large companies, this also means that the styling can be done by different people (e.g., graphic designers) who do not need to use the programmer’s development tools.

A style definition consists of two parts: a *selector* (the part before the curly brackets) and a set of *rules* in the brackets. The selector determines which components the definition applies to, and the rules define values for component properties.

The rules are typically easy to read: they always start with a “`–fx`” prefix, and their names suggest quite clearly the properties they set. We cannot list all available CSS properties here—there are far too many. To find out the names of the CSS properties, we look them up in the *JavaFX CSS Reference Guide*^([44](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:af12027f-1c48-4118-8aee-2241b51ce351)).

The selector used in the style definition above corresponds to a class name. Class selectors always start with a full stop, followed by the Java class name in lowercase, and with hyphens replacing mid-word capital letters (**Figure 17.19** shows some examples). You can also look up style class names for each component in the reference guide.

## 17.10.5: Defining your own style classes

If you have completed [**Exercise 17.62**](#urn_pearson_manifest_d324dedd-6b41-4d00-a1d6-ecf733232be5.xhtml), you may have noticed a limitation of using predefined class selectors: they always apply to all components of the class. If we use, for example, the `.label` selector, we are styling all labels. This is not always what we want—sometimes, we want to set a style for a specific label or a set of labels.

After [**Exercise 17.62**](#urn_pearson_manifest_d324dedd-6b41-4d00-a1d6-ecf733232be5.xhtml), you will see that the size of the menus and menu items has also changed in the same way the labels have. This is because the menu and menu item classes make use of labels to show their text on screen, so these labels are also affected. If we want to change only the size of the file path and status labels, then this cannot be done with the `.label` selector.

The solution to this problem is the definition of custom style classes. We can assign additional style classes to our components, and then we can write style definitions for those classes.

Let us look at an example.

**Code 17.15** adds the style class `infoLabel` to our two text labels. This class, `infoLabel`, does not exist—it is just a name for a new style class that we are defining here. (We have chosen the name “infoLabel” because these are the labels displaying information. You can choose any name you like, but as with naming all identifiers, try to make them descriptive.)

#### Code 17.15 **Assigning custom style classes to components**

Assigning this style class to the components has no immediate effect. It does, however, allow us to now add style definitions in our stylesheet for this class, and these definitions will apply only to these components.

Thus, in the stylesheet we can now write:

```
.infoLabel {
    -fx-font-size: 20px;
    -fx-padding: 12;
}
```

This definition will style only our two text labels.

You can, of course, use style classes for any set of components you like, so that you can style a group of components together to ensure they always have the same look.

## 17.10.6: Styling using ID selectors

The final thing we want to add in this version is padding around the toolbar buttons and the image. Currently, they are stuck right to the edge of the window, and that does not look nice. We do this by setting the `padding` and `spacing` properties of the layout panes. (*Padding* is space around the outside of the components of a layout pane, while *spacing* is space between the components.)

Layout panes do not have a predefined style class. This is because it almost never makes sense to apply styling to *all* `BorderPanes`, or to all instances of `VBox`. Instead, we shall use a *node ID*.

IDs can be assigned to any node (i.e., any JavaFX component) in the scene graph. Once we assign an ID, we can then write a style definition that only applies to the single component with that ID.

Let us do this for our toolbar. We can add a line to set the ID after we create the toolbar pane:

```
Pane toolBar = new VBox(smallerButton, largerButton);
toolBar.setId("toolbar");
```

We can then define a style for this ID:

```
#toolbar {
    -fx-padding: 12;
    -fx-spacing: 12;
}
```

As you can see, style selectors for IDs (as opposed to classes) start with a hash symbol (#) instead of a full stop.

The same ID can theoretically be used for multiple components (thus making ID selectors behave very similar to custom style classes), but this is discouraged. Use IDs when defining styles for single components, and style classes when styling groups of components.

All changes discussed so far are available in the book projects as *imageviewer3-0*. In that version, we have also added an additional filter called “Fish Eye” to give you an example of a more complex filter implementation. (The fish eye filter works best with portraits of people.)

*imageviewer4-0* shows examples of implementations of several other possible filters.

## 17.10.7: Inheriting styling

Styles set for any node in the scene graphs are inherited by all the nodes below it. To picture what this means, refer to the scene graph diagram in **Figure 17.14**: if we set an attribute for a component in this graph, the style will apply to that node and all children of that node (unless the children explicitly set the attribute as well). For example, if we set the font size for our toolbar (a VBox), this font size will automatically apply to all buttons in this tool bar. Thus, for consistency, it is often preferable to set properties for the whole pane than for individual controls.

The top level component (the one directly held in the scene), will automatically be assigned the style class `.root`. Thus, we can specify properties for the interface as a whole by writing rules for the `.root` class.

Try, for example, the following definition:

```
.root {
    -fx-font-size: 16pt;
    -fx-font-family: "Courier New";
    -fx-base: rgb(132, 145, 47);
    -fx-background: rgb(225, 228, 203);
}
```

When you run your program with these style rules, you will see that they apply to the whole interface, unless redefined for specific components.

## 17.10.8: Going further with styles

There is much more detail to discover about CSS styling, including compound selectors, pseudo classes, and a long, long list of properties. We will leave it to you to investigate the details over time. A very good starting point is the reference guide we referred to earlier. (You should probably bookmark it, if you have not yet done so.)

CSS styling is not a topic to study in completeness by reading the whole document. It is a rich and detailed area of which you will look up more and more details as you work on additional projects.

# 17.11: Further extensions

Programming GUIs with JavaFX is a big subject area. JavaFX has many different types of component and many different containers and layout managers. And each of these has many properties and methods.

Becoming familiar with the whole JavaFX library takes time, and is not something done in a few weeks. Usually, as we work on GUIs, we continue to read about details that we did not know before, and become experts over time.

The example discussed in this chapter, even though it contains a lot of detail, is only a brief introduction to GUI programming. We have discussed most of the important concepts, but there is still a large amount of functionality to be discovered, most of which is beyond the scope of this book.

Additional topics we have not covered here include:

*   Use of visual effects, such as shadows, reflections, lighting effects and transparency.
*   Animation, for example to move components in and out of the interface.
*   Use of GUI builders (such as Scene Builder^([45](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:00235475-50e9-4454-86a9-e62c7070b64b))) and FXML to build interfaces.

There are many sources of information available to help you continue. You frequently have to look up the API documentation for the JavaFX classes; it is not possible to work without it. There are also many GUI/JavaFX tutorials available, both in print and on the web.

Here are some exercises to get started with further investigation:

This is where we shall leave the discussion of the image viewer example. It can, however, be extended in many directions by interested readers. Using information from online documentation and tutorials, you can add numerous interface components.

The following exercises give you some ideas, and obviously there are many more possibilities.

# 17.12: Another example: MusicPlayer

So far in this chapter, we have discussed one example of a GUI application in detail. We now want to introduce a second application to provide another example to learn from. This program introduces a few additional GUI components.

This second example is a music-player application. We shall not discuss it in any great amount of detail. It is intended as a basis for studying the source code largely on your own and as a source of code fragments for you to copy and modify. Here, in this chapter, we shall only point out a few selected aspects of the application that are worth focusing on.

The *musicplayer* project provides a graphical interface to classes based on the *music-organizer* projects from [**Chapter 4**](#urn_pearson_manifest_2012b62f-6255-488f-89ab-7d7b6a88f14e.xhtml). As there, the program finds and plays MP3 files stored in the *audio* folder inside the chapter folder (one level up from the project folder). If you have sound files of the right format of your own, you should be able to play them by dropping them into the *audio* folder (Note that the artist/title display only works correctly if the file name has the right format.)

The music player is implemented across three classes: `MusicPlayer`, `PlayerEngine`, and `MusicFilePlayer`. Only the first is intended to be studied here. `MusicFilePlayer` can be used essentially as a library class; instances are created along with the name of the MP3 file to be played. Familiarize yourself with its interface, but you do not need to understand or modify its implementation. (You are welcome, of course, to study this class as well if you like, but it uses some concepts that we shall not discuss in this book.)

Following are some noteworthy observations about the *musicplayer* project.

**Model/view separation**

This application uses a better model/view separation than the previous example. This means that the application functionality (the model) is separated cleanly from the application’s user interface (the GUI). Each of those two, the model and the view, may consist of multiple classes, but every class should be clearly in one or the other group to achieve a clear separation. In our example, the view consists of a single class (the `MusicPlayer` class, which contains all of the GUI and not much else). You can see that no other class, for example, imports any JavaFX packages.

Separating the application’s functionality from the interface is an example of good cohesion; it makes the program easier to understand, easier to maintain, and easier to adapt to different requirements (especially different user interfaces). It would, for example, be fairly easy to write a text-based interface for the music player, effectively replacing the `MusicPlayer` class and leaving the other classes unchanged.

**Combo boxes**

The sound player presents an example of using a `ComboBox`. A combo box is a set of values, only one of which can be selected at any time. The selected value is displayed, and the selection can be accessed through a pop-up menu. In the sound player, the combo box is used to select a particular ordering for the tracks.

A `ComboBox` may also be editable, in which case the values are not all predefined but can be typed by a user. Ours is not.

**Lists**

The program also includes an example of a list (class `ListView`) for the list of tracks. A list can hold an arbitrary number of values, and one or more can be selected. The list values in this example are strings, but other types are possible.

**Mouse events and double-clicks**

We have included an example of a mouse event (to be precise: a mouse-clicked event). This is used for the track list: if you double-click a list item, the track will start to play. The event handler is actually invoked on every click in the list—you can study the event handler method to see how we make sure that only a double-click starts a track.

Other elements demonstrated in this example are the use of a slider (which does not do much at the moment—the implementation is missing), and the use of color for changing the look of an application.

# 17.13: Summary

In this chapter, we have supplied an introduction to GUI programming using JavaFX. We have discussed the three main conceptual areas: creating GUI components, layout, and event handling.

We have seen that building a GUI usually starts with creating a top-level window, which holds a scene. The scene is then filled with various components that provide information and functionality to the user. Among the components we have encountered are menus, menu items, buttons, labels and others.

Components are arranged on screen with the help of layout panes. Layout panes hold collections of components and take care of arranging the components within the pane’s screen area. Nesting layout panes, using combinations of different panes, is a common way to achieve the desired combination of component size and juxtaposition.

Controls (interactive components that can react to user input) generate events when they are activated by a user. We can specify event listener methods which are notified of such events when they occur. When the listener method is notified, it can take appropriate action to deal with the user event. Event listeners are typically implemented using method references or lambda notation.

And finally, we have given pointers to online references and tutorials that may be used to learn about details not covered in the chapter.

Terms introduced in this chapter:

1.  **GUI, JavaFX, stage, scene, scene graph, component, control, layout, layout pane, event, event handling, event listener, label, button, menu bar, menu, menu item, modal dialog, styling, CSS**

# Chapter 18 Handling Errors

In [**Chapter 9**](#urn_pearson_manifest_e31c32ee-61ad-45d5-b813-f0c6d945c289.xhtml), we saw that logical errors in programs are harder to spot than syntactical errors, because a compiler cannot give any help with logical errors. Logical errors arise for several reasons, which may overlap in some situations:

*   The solution to a problem has been implemented incorrectly. For instance, a problem involving generating some statistics on data values might have been programmed to find the mean value rather than the median value (the “middle” value).
*   An object might be asked to do something it is unable to. For instance, a collection object’s `get` method might be called with an index value outside the valid range.
*   An object might be used in ways that have not been anticipated by the class designer, leading to the object being left in an inconsistent or inappropriate state. This often happens when a class is reused in a setting that is different from its original one, perhaps having been extended through inheritance.

Although the sort of testing strategies discussed in [**Chapter 9**](#urn_pearson_manifest_e31c32ee-61ad-45d5-b813-f0c6d945c289.xhtml) can help us identify and eliminate many logical errors before our programs are put to use, experience suggests that program failures will continue to occur. Furthermore, even the most thoroughly tested program may fail as a result of circumstances beyond the programmer’s control. Consider the case of a web-browser asked to display a web page when the network connection has been lost, or a program that tries to write data to a disk that has no more space left. These problems are not the result of logical programming errors, but they could easily cause a program to fail if the possibility of their arising has not been considered.

In this chapter, we look at how to anticipate potential errors and how to respond to error situations as they arise during the execution of a program. In addition, we provide some suggestions on how to report errors when they occur. We also provide a brief introduction to how to perform input/output, as file processing is one of the situations where errors can easily arise.

# 18.1: The address book project

We shall use the *address-book* family of projects to illustrate some of the principles of error reporting and error handling that arise in many applications. The projects represent an application that stores personal contact details—name, address, and phone number—for an arbitrary number of people. Such a contacts list might be used on a mobile phone or in an email program, for instance. The contact details are indexed in the address book by both name and phone number. The main classes we shall discuss are `AddressBook` (**Code 18.1**) and `ContactDetails`. In addition, the `AddressBookDemo` class is provided as a convenient means of setting up an initial address book with some sample data.

New details can be stored in the address book via its `addDetails` method. This assumes that the details represent a new contact, and not a change of details for an existing one. To cover the latter case, the `changeDetails` method removes an old entry and replaces it with the revised details. The address book provides two ways to retrieve entries: the `getDetails` method takes a name or phone number as the key and returns the matching details; the `search` method returns an array of all those details that start with a given search string (for instance, the search string `"084"` would return all entries with phone numbers having that prefix).

There are two introductory versions of the *address-book* project for you to explore. Both provide access to the same version of `AddressBook`, as shown in **Code 18.1**. The *address-book-v1t* project provides a text-based user interface, similar in style to the interface of the *zuul* game discussed in [**Chapter 8**](#urn_pearson_manifest_bbb77ecc-45b8-45de-8fb1-efd5b55e0711.xhtml). Commands are currently available to list the address book’s contents, search it, and add a new entry. Probably more interesting as an interface, however, is the *address-book-v1g* version, which incorporates a simple GUI. Experiment with both versions to gain some experience with what the application can do.

# 18.2: Defensive programming

## 18.2.1: Client–server interaction

An `AddressBook` is a typical *server* *class*. In other words, its objects respond to calls to their methods from other objects and initiate no actions on their own. All of a server object's actions are driven by calls from other objects, which we call *client objects*. Programmers can adopt at least two possible views when designing and implementing a server class:

*   They can assume that the client classes have been written accurately, so that the client objects only ever interact with the server objects in a sensible and well-defined way.
*   They can assume that server objects will operate in an essentially problematic environment in which all possible steps must be taken to prevent client objects from using them incorrectly.

These views clearly represent opposite extremes. In practice, the most likely scenario usually lies somewhere in between. Most client interactions will be reasonable, with the occasional attempt to use the server incorrectly—either as the result of a logical programming error or of misconception on the part of the programmer of the client classes. A third possibility, of course, is an intentionally hostile client that is trying to break or find a weakness in the server class.

These different views provide a useful base from which to discuss questions such as:

*   How much checking for inappropriate use should a server class have built into its methods?
*   How should a server method report an error to its client caller?
*   How can a client caller anticipate failure of a method call?
*   How should a client deal with failure of one of its calls?

If we examine the `AddressBook` class with these issues in mind, we shall see that the class has been written to trust completely that its clients will call its methods appropriately. **Exercise 18.8** illustrates how things can go wrong given this assumption.

The problem with the `removeDetails` method is that it assumes that the key passed to it is a valid key for the address book. It uses the supposed key to retrieve the associated contact details:

```
ContactDetails details = book.get(key);
```

However, if the map does not have that particular key, then the `details` variable ends up containing `null`. That, of itself, is not an error; but the error arises from the following statement, where we assume that `details` refers to a valid object:

```
book.remove(details.name());
```

It is an error to call a method on a variable containing `null`, and the result will be a run-time error. BlueJ reports this as a `NullPointerException` and highlights the statement from which it resulted. In the Terminal window, a diagnostic message explains the reason for the error:

```
Cannot invoke "ContactDetails.name()" because "details" is null
```

Later in this chapter, we shall discuss *exceptions* in detail. For now, we can simply say that, if an error such as this were to occur in a running application, then the application would crash—that is, terminate in an uncontrolled way—before it had completed its task.

There is clearly a problem here, but whose fault is it? Is it the fault of the writer of the client class, for calling the `removeDetails` method with a bad parameter value, or is it the fault of the writer of the server class for failing to anticipate and handle this situation properly? The writer of the client class might argue that there is nothing in the method’s documentation to say that the key must be valid. Conversely, the writer of the server class might argue that it is obviously wrong to try to remove details with an invalid key. Our concern in this chapter is not to resolve such disputes, but to try to prevent them from arising in the first place. We shall start by looking at error handling from the point of view of the server class.

## 18.2.2: Parameter checking

A server object is most vulnerable when its constructor and methods receive values through their parameters. The values passed to a constructor are used to set up an object’s initial state, while the values passed to a method will be used to influence the overall effect of the method call and may change the state of the object and a result the method returns. Therefore, it is vital that a server object knows whether it can trust parameter values to be valid, or whether it needs to check their validity for itself. The current situation in both the `ContactDetails` and `AddressBook` classes is that there is no checking at all on parameter values. As we have seen with the `removeDetails` method, this can lead to a fatal runtime error.

Preventing a `NullPointerException` in `removeDetails` is relatively easy, and **Code 18.2** illustrates how this can be done. Note that, as well as improving the source code in the method, we have updated the method’s comment, to document the fact that unknown keys are ignored.

# 18.3: Server error reporting

Having protected a server object from performing an illegal operation through bad parameter values, we could take the view that this is all that the server writer needs to do. However, ideally, we would like to avoid such error situations from arising in the first place. Furthermore, it is often the case that incorrect parameter values are the result of some form of programming error in the client class that supplied them. Therefore, rather than simply programming around the problem in the server and leaving it at that, it is good practice for the server object to make some effort to indicate that a problem has arisen, either to the client object itself or to a human user or programmer. In that way, there is a chance that an incorrectly written client will be fixed. But notice that those three “audiences” for the notification will often be completely different.

What is the best way for a server to report problems when they occur? There is no single answer to this question, and the most appropriate answer will often depend upon the context in which a particular server object is being used. In the following sections, we shall explore a range of options for error reporting by a server.

## 18.3.1: Notifying the user

The most obvious way in which an object might respond when it detects something wrong is to try to notify the application’s user in some way. The main options are to print an error message using `System.out` or `System.err`, or to display an error message alert window.

The two main problems with both approaches are:

*   They assume that the application is being used by a human user who will see the error message. There are many applications that run completely independently of a human user. An error message, or an error window, will go completely unnoticed. Indeed, the computer running the application might not have any visual-display device connected to it at all.
*   Even where there is a human user to see the error message, it will be rare for that user to be in a position to do something about the problem. Imagine a user at an automatic teller machine being confronted with a `NullPointerException`! Only in those cases where the user’s direct action has led to the problem—such as supplying invalid input to the application—is the user likely to be able take some appropriate corrective or avoiding action the next time.

Programs that print inappropriate error messages are more likely to annoy their users rather than achieve a useful outcome. Therefore, except in a very limited set of circumstances, notifying the user is not a general solution to the problem of error reporting.

## 18.3.2: Notifying the client object

A radically different approach from those we have discussed so far is for the server object to feedback an indication to the client object when something has gone wrong. There are two main ways to do this:

*   A server can use a non-`void` return type of a method to return a value that indicates either success or failure of the method call.
*   A server can *throw an exception* if something goes wrong. This introduces a new feature of Java that is also found in some other programming languages. We shall describe this feature in detail in [**Section 18.4**](#urn_pearson_manifest_773a5fa0-4e45-42b4-9e77-6168c38aa1b0.xhtml).

Both techniques have the benefit of encouraging the programmer of the *client* to consider that a method call could fail. However, only the decision to throw an exception will actively prevent the client’s programmer from ignoring the consequences of method failure.

The first approach is easy to introduce to a method that would otherwise have a `void` return type, such as `removeDetails`. If the `void` type is replaced by a `boolean` type, then the method can return `true` to indicate that the removal was successful, and `false` to indicate that it failed for some reason (**Code 18.3**).

This will be the case if a value from the return type’s range is available to act as an error diagnostic value. // Send David a text message.

String phone = details.phone();

Line 15: Indentation level 2, CloseCurlyBracket

Line 16: CloseCurlyBracket

This would allow a client to examine the result of the call, then either continue with the normal flow of control or attempt to recover from the error:

```
ContactDetails details = contacts.getDetails("David");
if(details != null) {
    // Send a text message to David.
    String phone = details.phone();
    ...
}
else {
    // Failed to find the entry.
    // Attempt a recovery, if possible.
    ...
}
```

It is common for methods that return object references to use the `null` value as an indication of failure or error. With methods that return primitive-type values, there will sometimes be an *out-of-bounds value* that can fulfill a similar role: for instance, the `indexOf` method of the `String` class returns a negative value to indicate that it has failed to find the character sought.

Clearly, an out-of-bounds value cannot be used where all values from the return type already have valid meanings to the client. In addition, there is no way *to require* the client to check the return value for its diagnostic properties. As a consequence, if a null value is returned to indicate a problem, for instance, then a client could easily carry on as if nothing has happened and could then end up terminating with a `NullPointerException`. Or where an out-of-bounds primitive value is returned, the client might even use the diagnostic return value as if it were a normal return value, potentially creating a difficult-to-diagnose logical error!

In effect, we may be using the diagnostic value for two quite different purposes. One purpose is to tell the client whether its request was successful or not. The other is to indicate that there was something wrong with its request, such as passing bad parameter values. This is the case in the revised `getDetails` (**Code 18.4**) and `removeDetails` (**Code 18.3**) methods. In `getDetails`, a null result represents an unsuccessful request, where the result simply indicates that no details were found for the given parameter. In `removeDetails`, however, a null result represents an incorrect request—a programmer error—since the comment explicitly states that the key should be in use.

In many cases, an *unsuccessful* request will not represent a logical programming error, whereas an *incorrect* request almost certainly does. We should expect quite different follow-up actions from a client in those different situations, so alternative ways than those discussed so far will sometimes be needed for a server object to inform its client that it is unable to do what it has been asked to.

In [Section 18.3.3](#urn_pearson_manifest_2ad6dc08-cd03-4991-8ed0-3e0d5c7bdfa8.xhtml), we discuss how to report an unsuccessful method call and in [Section 18.4](#urn_pearson_manifest_773a5fa0-4e45-42b4-9e77-6168c38aa1b0.xhtml) we discuss how to report an incorrect method call.

## 18.3.3: The Optional type

In [**Section 5.6.6**](#urn_pearson_manifest_cefc7fc0-9353-4155-bc8c-08c2de290dd0.xhtml), we introduced the `Optional` class, from the `java.util` package, as a way for a stream pipeline to return either a meaningful result or to indicate that no result is available. Optional objects either wrap the item sought, or they are *empty*. Being empty is not the same as storing a null value. An Optional object has `isEmpty` and `isPresent` methods for the receiving object to check whether they are empty or do contain a meaningful value.

This exactly fits the requirements we have been discussing for how a server object can indicate to its client that there was nothing wrong with their call, but there is no useful result from the call. For a successful call, the `isPresent` method will return true but for an unsuccessful call it will return false and `isEmpty` will return true.

The consequence of this is the client will be forced to check the result of an operation that returns an Optional, and then either extract the object/value stored in the Optional object, or to take an appropriate action if the Optional is empty.

**Code 18.5** shows a version of the `removeDetails` method that uses the static `ofNullable` method of the `Optional` class to return an Optional object containing the removed `ContactDetails`, if present, but an empty object if there was no match. Note that, even though `null` is passed to the `ofNullable` method when there is no match, the Optional object will not store `null` in that case. The `null` value is simply used to indicate that there is no `ContactDetails` object to be stored in the Optional object and that it is empty.

The Optional type is an ideal lightweight way for a server object to clearly indicate to a client object the success or failure of a request for data.

# 18.4: Exception-throwing principles

Throwing an exception is the most effective way a server object has of indicating that it is unable to fulfill a call on one of its methods. One of the major advantages this has over using a special return value is that it is (almost) impossible for a client to ignore the fact that an exception has been thrown and carry on regardless. Failure by the client to handle an exception will result in the application terminating immediately.^([46](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:5ff08f9c-a777-496e-bbe4-f39a605558e0)) In addition, the exception mechanism is independent of the return value of a method, so it can be used for all methods, irrespective of the return type.

Throwing an exception is a relatively heavyweight option for indicating a failure, in contrast to returning an Optional object, and it should be used for logical errors or unrecoverable failures rather than simply the failure to find something, for instance.

An important point to bear in mind throughout the following discussion is that, where exceptions are involved, the place where an error is discovered will be distinct from where recovery (if any) is attempted. Discovery will be in the server’s method, and recovery will be in the client. If recovery were possible at the point of discovery, then there would be no point in throwing an exception.

There are two stages to throwing an exception. First, an exception object is created using the `new` keyword (in this case, an `IllegalArgumentException` object); then the exception object is thrown using the `throw` keyword. These two stages are almost invariably combined in a single statement:

```
throw new ExceptionType("optional-diagnostic-string");
```

When an exception object is created, a diagnostic string may be passed to its constructor. This string is later available to the receiver of the exception via the exception object’s `getMessage` and `toString` methods. The string is also shown to the user if the exception is not handled and leads to the termination of the program. The exception type we have used here, `IllegalArgumentException`, is defined in the `java.lang` package and is regularly used to indicate that an inappropriate argument value has been passed to a method or constructor.

**Code 18.6** also illustrates that the `javadoc` documentation for a method can be expanded to include details of any exceptions it throws using the `@throws` tag.

## 18.4.2: Checked and unchecked exceptions

An exception object is always an instance of a class from a special inheritance hierarchy. We can create new exception types by creating subclasses in this hierarchy (**Figure 18.1**). Strictly speaking, exception classes are always subclasses of the `Throwable` class that is defined in the `java.lang` package. We shall follow the convention of defining and using exception classes that are subclasses of the `Exception` class, also defined in `java.lang`.^([47](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:9b27402c-bb6e-41c8-954d-f944abe2b055)) That package defines a number of commonly seen exception classes that you might already have encountered while developing programs, such as `NullPointerException`, `IndexOutOfBoundsException`, and `ClassCastException`.

#### Figure 18.1 **The exception class hierarchy**

![A flowchart depicts the hierarchy of the exception class from bottom to top with shaded boxes representing standard library classes and unshaded boxes representing user-defined classes.](images/9c5980be-2c23-4755-b6e7-fa1edce308c2_ASSET_FG_18_001-1.png "View Image")

An unshaded box labeled MyUncheckedException is positioned at the bottom. An arrow extends from this box to the upper right, pointing to a shaded box labeled RuntimeException. The RuntimeException box has an arrow pointing to the upper left, leading to another shaded box labeled Exception. To the right of the RuntimeException box, an unshaded box labeled MyCheckedException is shown. This box has an arrow pointing to the upper right, which also leads to the Exception box. The Exception box, in turn, has an arrow pointing to the upper left, leading to a shaded box labeled Throwable. Additionally, to the left of the Exception box, there is another shaded box labeled Error, which also points to the Throwable box.

Java divides exception classes into two categories: *checked exceptions* and *unchecked exceptions.* All subclasses of the Java standard class `RuntimeException` are unchecked exceptions; all other subclasses of `Exception` are checked exceptions.

Slightly simplified, the difference is this: checked exceptions are intended for cases where the client should expect that an operation could fail (e.g., if it tries to write to a disk, it should anticipate that the disk could be full). In such cases, the client will be forced to check whether the operation was successful. Unchecked exceptions are intended for cases that should never fail in normal operation—they usually indicate a program error. For instance, a programmer would never knowingly try to get an item from a position in a list that does not exist, so when they do, it elicits an unchecked exception.

Unfortunately, knowing which category of exception to throw in any particular circumstance is not an exact science, but we can offer the following general advice:

*   One rule of thumb is to use unchecked exceptions for situations that should lead to program failure—typically because it is suspected that there is a logical error in the program that will prevent it from continuing any further. It follows that checked exceptions should be used where there may be a possibility of the client effecting a recovery. One problem with this policy is that it assumes that the server is aware enough of the context in which it is being used to be able to determine whether client recovery is likely or unlikely to be possible.
*   Another rule of thumb is to use unchecked exceptions for situations that could reasonably be avoided. For instance, calling a method on a variable containing `null` is the result of a logical programming error that is completely avoidable, and the fact that `NullPointerException` is unchecked fits this model. It follows that checked exceptions should be used for failure situations that are beyond the control of the programmer, such as a disk becoming full when trying to write to a file or a network operation failing because a wireless network connection has dropped out.

The formal Java rules governing the use of exceptions are significantly different for unchecked and checked exceptions, and we shall outline the differences in detail in [**Sections 18.4.4**](#urn_pearson_manifest_f11c3412-3bce-45e6-9889-f8f90f18fc66.xhtml) and [**18.5.1**](#urn_pearson_manifest_27bd268c-f8d9-41c2-981b-9cd406e7d82c.xhtml), respectively. In simplified terms, the rules ensure that a client object calling a method that could throw a checked exception will contain code that anticipates the possibility of a problem arising and that attempts to handle the problem whenever it occurs.^([48](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:650f3c15-6447-4a54-aa24-83e5778fbcc7))

## 18.4.3: The effect of an exception

What happens when an exception is thrown? There are really two effects to consider: the effect in the method where the problem is discovered, and the effect in the caller of the method.

When an exception is thrown, the execution of the throwing method finishes immediately; it does not continue to the end of the method body. A consequence of this is that a method with a non-`void` return type is not required to execute a return statement on a route that throws an exception. This is reasonable, because throwing an exception is an indication of the throwing method’s inability to continue normal execution, which includes not being able to return a valid result. We can illustrate this principle with the following alternative version of the method body shown in **Code 18.6**:

```
if(key == null) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                  "null key in getDetails");
}
else {
    return book.get(key);
}
```

The absence of a return statement in the route that throws an exception is acceptable. Indeed, the compiler will indicate an error if any statements are written following a throw statement, because they could never be executed.

The effect of an exception on the point in the program that called the problem method is a little more complex. In particular, the full effect depends upon whether or not any code has been written to *catch* the exception. Consider the following contrived call to `getDetails`:

```
AddressDetails details = contacts.getDetails(null);
// The following statement will not be reached.
String phone = details.phone();
```

We *can* say that, in all cases, the execution of these statements will be left incomplete; the exception thrown by `getDetails` will interrupt the execution of the first statement, and no assignment will be made to the `details` variable. As a result, the second statement will not be executed either.

This neatly illustrates the power of exceptions to prevent a client from carrying on, regardless of the fact that a problem has arisen. What actually happens next depends upon whether or not the exception is caught. If it isn’t caught, then the program will simply terminate with an indication that an uncaught `IllegalArgumentException` has been thrown. We shall discuss how to catch an exception in [**Section 18.5.2**](#urn_pearson_manifest_7bbb2802-41db-4cf1-b25e-b928a2117226.xhtml).

## 18.4.4: Using unchecked exceptions

Unchecked exceptions are the easiest to use from a programmer’s point of view because the compiler enforces few rules on their use. This is the meaning of *unchecked*: the compiler does not apply special checks, either on the method in which an unchecked exception is thrown or on the place from which the method is called. An exception class is unchecked if it is a subclass of the `RuntimeException` class. All of the examples we have used so far to illustrate exception throwing have involved unchecked exceptions. So, there is little further to add here about how to throw an unchecked exception—simply use a throw statement.

If we also follow the convention that unchecked exceptions should be used in those situations where we expect the result to be program termination—that is, the exception is not going to be caught—then there is also nothing further to be discussed about what the method’s caller should do, because it will do nothing and let the program fail. However, if there is a need to catch an unchecked exception, then an exception handler *can* be written for it, exactly as for a checked exception. How to do this is described in [**Section 18.5.2**](#urn_pearson_manifest_7bbb2802-41db-4cf1-b25e-b928a2117226.xhtml).

We have already seen use of the unchecked `IllegalArgumentException`; this is thrown by a constructor or method to indicate that its parameter values are inappropriate. For instance, the `getDetails` method might also choose to throw this if the key string passed to it is blank (**Code 18.7**).

It is well worth having a method conduct a series of validity checks on its parameters before proceeding with the main purpose of the method. This makes it less likely that a method will get partway through its actions before having to throw an exception because of bad parameter values. A particular reason for avoiding this situation is that partial mutation of an object is likely to leave it in an inconsistent state for future use. If a method fails for any reason, the object on which it was called should ideally be left in the state it was before the operation was attempted.

The static `requireNonNull` method of the `java.util.Objects` class provides a convenient shorthand for testing an expression and throwing an exception if the expression is `null`. The following will throw a `NullPointerException`, with the associated string, if the value of `key` is `null`; otherwise it will do nothing:

```
Objects.requireNonNull(key, "null key passed to getDetails");
```

## 18.4.5: Preventing object creation

An important use for exceptions is to prevent objects from being created if they cannot be placed in a valid initial state. This will usually be the result of inappropriate parameter values being received by a constructor. We can illustrate this with the `ContactDetails` class. The constructor is currently fairly forgiving of the parameter values it receives; it does not reject `null` values but replaces them with empty strings. However, the address book needs at least a name or phone number from each entry to use as a unique index value, so an entry with both `name` and `phone` fields blank would be impossible to index. We can reflect this requirement by preventing construction of a `ContactDetails` object with no valid key details. The process of throwing an exception from a constructor is exactly the same as throwing one from a method. **Code 18.8** shows the revised constructor that will prevent an entry from ever having both `name` and `phone` fields blank.

# 18.5: Exception handling

The principles of exception throwing apply equally to unchecked and checked exceptions, but the rules of Java mean that exception handling is a requirement only with checked exceptions. A checked exception class is one that is a subclass of `Exception`, but not of `RuntimeException`. There are several more rules to follow when using checked exceptions, because the compiler enforces checks both in a method that throws a checked exception and in any caller of that method.

## 18.5.1: Checked exceptions: the throws clause

The first requirement of the compiler is that a method throwing a checked exception must declare that it does so in a *throws clause* added to the method’s header. For instance, a method throwing a checked `IOException` from the `java.io` package might have the following header:^([49](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:4601e4e7-5645-4011-b725-93a0fd1af269))

```
public void saveToFile(String destinationFile)
    throws IOException
```

It is permitted to use a throws clause for unchecked exceptions, but the compiler does not require one. We recommend that a throws clause be used only to list the checked exceptions thrown by a method.

It is important to distinguish between a throws clause in the header of a method, and the `@throws` javadoc comment that precedes the method; the latter is completely optional for both types of exception. Nevertheless, we recommend that javadoc documentation be included for both checked and unchecked exceptions. In that way, as much information as possible will be available to someone wishing to use a method that throws an exception.

## 18.5.2: Anticipating exceptions: the try statement

The second requirement, when using checked exceptions, is that a caller of a method that throws a checked exception must make provision for dealing with the exception. This usually means writing an *exception handler* in the form of a *try statement*. Most practical try statements have the general form shown in **Code 18.9**. This introduces two new Java keywords—`try` and `catch`—which mark a *try block* and a *catch block*, respectively.

#### Code 18.9 **The try and catch blocks of an exception handler**

![A program code is shown with a try and a catch block.](images/760c4746-869b-4b26-a3e8-732b01cc9c53_ASSET_Code_18_009.jpg "View Image")

The code has the following lines:

Suppose we have a method that saves the contents of an address book to a file. The user is requested in some way for the name of a file (perhaps via a GUI dialog window), and the address book’s `saveToFile` method is then called to write out the list to the file. If we did not have to take exceptions into account, then this would be written as follows:

```
String filename = request-a-file-from-the-user;
addressbook.saveToFile(filename);
```

However, because the writing process could fail with an exception, the call to `saveToFile` must be placed within a try block to show that this has been considered. **Code 18.10** illustrates how we would tend to write this, anticipating possible failure.

Any number of statements can be included in a try block, so we tend to place there not just the single statement that could fail, but all of the statements that are related to it in some way. The idea is that a try block represents a sequence of actions we wish to treat as a logical whole but recognize that they might fail at some point.^([50](#urn_pearson_manifestation_0ae6c350-3b3e-4d0f-8d7b-2a01f9a52bf0.xhtml_urn:pearson:work:597b9d6a-ab4f-4d83-a358-df4cf445a87c)) The catch block will then attempt to deal with the situation or report the problem if an exception arises from any statement within the associated try block. Note that, because both the try and catch blocks make use of the `filename` and `successful` variables, they have to be declared outside the try statement in this example, for reasons of scope.

In order to understand how an exception handler works, it is essential to appreciate that *an exception prevents the normal flow of control from being continued in the caller*. An exception interrupts the execution of the caller’s statements, and hence any statements immediately following the problem statement will not be executed. The question then arises, “Where is execution resumed in the caller?” A try statement provides the answer: if an exception arises from a statement in the try block, then execution is resumed in the corresponding catch block. So, if we consider the example in **Code 18.10**, the effect of an `IOException` being thrown from the call to `saveToFile` will be that control will transfer from the try block to the catch block, as shown in **Code 18.11**.

#### Code 18.11 **Transfer of control in a try statement**

![A program code with the expectation handler shows the transfer control.](images/7e30453d-8ef0-49a6-a2e1-29c22a100651_ASSET_Code_18_011.jpg "View Image")

The code has the following lines:

Line 1: try OpenCurlyBracket

Line 2: Indentation level 1, filename equals request hyphen a hyphen file hyphen from hyphen the hyphen user semicolon

Line 3: Indentation level 1, addressBook dot saveToFile OpenParenthesis filename CloseParenthesis semicolon

Line 4: Indentation level 1, successful equals true semicolon

Line 5: CloseCurlyBracket

Line 6: catch OpenParenthesis IOException e CloseParenthesis OpenCurlyBracket

Line 8: Indentation level 1, successful equals false semicolon

Line 9: CloseCurlyBracket

An arrow points to line 7 and labeled is labeled “1 dot Exception thrown from here.” An arrow points to line 7 and labeled “2 dot Control transfers here dot.”

Statements in a try block are known as *protected statements*. If no exception arises during execution of protected statements, then the catch block will be skipped over when the end of the try block is reached. Execution will continue with whatever follows the complete try/catch statement.

A catch block names the type of exception it is designed to deal with in a pair of parentheses immediately following the `catch` word. As well as the exception type name, this also includes a variable name (traditionally, simply `e` or `ex`) that can be used to refer to the exception object that was thrown. Having a reference to this object can be useful in providing information that will support recovery from, or reporting of, the problem—for example, accessing any diagnostic message placed in it by the throwing method. Once the catch block has been completed, control does *not* return to the statement that caused the exception.

Note that in all the examples of try statements you have seen, the exception is not thrown *directly* by the statements in the try block, which is in the client object. Rather, the exception arises *indirectly*, passed back from a method in the server object, which is called from the statements within the try block. This is the usual pattern, and it would almost certainly be a programming error to enclose a throw statement directly within a try statement.

## 18.5.3: Throwing and catching multiple exceptions

Sometimes a method throws more than one type of exception in order to indicate different sorts of problems. Where these are checked exceptions, they must all be listed in the throws clause of the method, separated by commas. For instance:

```
public void process()
    throws EOFException, FileNotFoundException
```

An exception handler must cater for all checked exceptions thrown from its protected statements, so a try statement may contain multiple catch blocks, as shown in **Code 18.12**. Note that the same variable name can be used for the exception object in each case.

#### Code 18.12 **Multiple catch blocks in a try statement**

![A program code with multiple catch blocks is shown.](images/412bea4a-dd61-43a5-a6a4-f5b1ae147b66_ASSET_Code_18_012.png "View Image")

The code has the following lines:

Line 1: try OpenCurlyBracket

Line 2: Indentation level 1, horizontal ellipsis

Line 3: Indentation level 1, ref dot process OpenParenthesis CloseParenthesis semicolon

Line 4: Indentation level 1, horizontal ellipsis

Line 5: CloseCurlyBracket

Line 6: catch OpenParenthesis EOFException e CloseParenthesis OpenCurlyBracket

Line 7: Indentation level 1, DoubleForwardSlash Take appropriate action for an end-of-file exception

Line 8: Indentation level 1, horizontal ellipsis

Line 9: CloseCurlyBracket

Line 10: catch OpenParenthesis FileNotFoundException e CloseParenthesis OpenCurlyBracket

Line 11: Indentation level 1, DoubleForwardSlash Take appropriate action for a file-not- found exception

Line 12: Indentation level 1, horizontal ellipsis

Line 13: CloseCurlyBracket

When an exception is thrown, the catch blocks are checked in the order in which they are written until a match is found for the exception type. So, if an `EOFException` is thrown, then control will transfer to the first catch block, and if a `FileNotFoundException` is thrown, then control will transfer to the second. Once the end of a single catch block is reached, execution continues following the last catch block.

Polymorphism can be used to avoid writing multiple catch blocks, if desired. However, this could be at the expense of being able to take type-specific recovery actions. In **Code 18.13**, the single catch block will handle *every* exception thrown by the protected statements. This is because the exception-matching process that looks for an appropriate catch block simply checks that the exception object is an instance of the type named in the block. As all exceptions are subtypes of the `Exception` class, the single block will catch everything, whether checked or unchecked. From the nature of the matching process, it follows that the order of catch blocks in a single try statement matters, and that a catch block for one exception type cannot follow a block for one of its supertypes because the earlier supertype block will always match before the subtype block is checked. The compiler will report this as an error.
